title: Fitting slimline kitchen wallcupboard pelmet. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-775963136", "author_name": "HU-775963136", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-775963136", "date": "2022-03-01", "text": "Hi, Working on my first DIY kitchen refurb and am ready to place order for all parts. Fairly long lead time so I want to get it right first time !  I am keeping all carcasses and putting new doors, end panels etc in place. I want to have a slimline pelmet top and bottom of wall cupboards. The end panels are 18mm+Acrylic but all the pelmets from the various manufacturers are 30mm or more. Is there any reason not to use standard plinth material as a pelmet ? It is 18mm+acrylic also and I reckon will look rather neat.  It will be of uniform appearance  in that the side panels and the top and bottom all will the the same width. Sorry if its a daft question but since I find no mention of this anywhere on the web I am wondering if there is some daft reason I have overlooked why this shouldn't be done. Ta! Angela", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jonathandb1972", "author_name": "Jonathan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jonathandb1972", "date": "2022-03-01", "text": "It sounds like you have a good and clear plan you are just using the wrong word for what you mean. You want to put a panel top and bottom to match the sides.   So you need a top and bottom panel and if your manufacturer doesn\u2019t produce that you want to give the illusion of it from the front by using a different component such as plinth. You just need to satisfy yourself that they are made of the same stuff as plinth is often lower quality. A pelmet is usually used to hide something such as under cabinet lights and that is why it is bigger than a panel.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-775963136", "author_name": "HU-775963136", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-775963136", "date": "2022-03-03", "text": "Thanks for that encouraging reply. I checked with the manufacturer  and am told that the plinth is made exactly the same as the other panelling and is suitable for filler or  use as a kind of pelmet. Incidentally I am intending to hide some LED lighting behind the narrow 18mm plinth/pelmet/panel and am aware there is not much room, but I have used bare adhesive LED strip before and am handy with an electronic soldering iron so this shouldn't be a problem. Kind Regards Angela", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "lifestyle-kitchens-pfvwgb-pf~1385883894", "author_name": "Lifestyle Kitchens", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/kitchen-designers-and-remodelers/lifestyle-kitchens-pfvwgb-pf~1385883894", "date": "2022-03-03", "text": "There's absolutely nothing wrong with what you suggest and its something i do quite often when ordering but as @Jonathan says not only the plinth can sometimes be made of different material, but the back can sometimes be a completely different colour, so i usually order decor panel with a matching edge (i assume when you say its acrylic you have the choice of 2 tone or matching edge) and this i can order at 100mm width (or smaller if i can). other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "hoosier-nan", "author_name": "hoosier_nan (IN z5b/6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hoosier-nan", "date": "2022-03-01", "text": "Here's what we do to prevent damping off. Keep in mind that damp/moist are the operational words for how much water should be in the medium; and, if your pot is deeper than about 5\", the commonly offered advice to \"water when the top inch or two of the soil feels dry to your touch\" is inappropriate, as it is a recipe for over-watering. There is some chance that the spoiled foliage is from under-watering or a high level of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from fertilizer solutions and the minerals dissolved in tapwater, but there isn't enough information to determine that yet. Still the advice I offered about getting watering intervals right applies. If you water while you can still detect some moisture in the medium either by visual confirmation or testing it with a finger, you're not under-watering. Also, if you haven't noticed the plant wilting, it's very unlikely under-watering is to blame. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2022-03-01", "text": "I'm not sure what the question is.  The function of hoods is capture and containment (and fire blocking).  Normally, one wants the area that collects rising and expanding cooking effluent plumes to overlap both front and back burner plumes to ensure capture.  One wants the air flow rate (CFM) to be sufficient to ensure that any such captured plumes remain captured, that is, do not escape before being ejected to the outdoors. Very modest devices such as that at the link might successfully deal with lightly simmering bacon, soup simmering, fish poaching, so long as the mesh filters are kept clean.  For any intent to capture and contain the plumes from hot oil cooking up to and including wok cooking and meat searing, a significantly more capable hood is required. title: hood cabinet symmetry vs. alignment with base cabinets | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jonathan-watts50", "author_name": "Jonathan Watts", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jonathan-watts50", "date": "2022-03-02", "text": "*Original plan had 2 18\u201d cabinets flanking a decorative hood.*Designer didn\u2019t account for filler next blind corner and didn\u2019t account for end panels on cabinets.*with only 1/2\u201d filler, keeping 18\u201d cabinet to the right of the hood would have resulted in the hood being 1/2\u201d off center from the range.*as a compromise to requiring a new, longer corner cabinet, I agreed with contractor that they could order 2 17\u201d cabinets to flank the hood.*without my approval, they decided to order 1 16.5\u201d cabinet to replace the 18\u201d cabinet with to the right of the hood.*the pictures show 1 18\u201d cabinet on the left and one 16.5\u201d cabinet on the right.*my wife wanted this to be a feature wall and the decorative wood hood was very expensive.  She is insisting on symmetry.  We are compromising again and asking the contractor to order the 16.5\u201d cabinet for the left of the stove.  They are leaving 1/2\u201d filler and we will use a 110 to 85 degree hinge angle restrictor.*the 16.5\u201d cabinet plus 2 end panels will be 1.75\u201d to the right of the end of the countertop and will 1.25\u201d to the right of the end of the 23\u201d base cabinet with decorative end panel. ***the two tiles stacked lengthwise in the pic represent the location where the 16.5\u201d cabinet would end.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/17626fd7021ee840_2709-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "rebunky", "author_name": "rebunky", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rebunky", "date": "2022-03-02", "text": "I am pretty ocd about having symmetry, so I get where your wife is coming from. But honestly, in your particular kitchen layout, even if those two cabinets were equal sizes at 18\u201d, my eye would not pick up on them being symmetrical. Hopefully I can explain what I mean. The left cabinet is all by itself.  The right cabinet connects to the adjacent cabinetry, which connects to that long wall of cabinets.  So you don\u2019t really see the right side as a single cabinet that needs to match the left.  Another thing is because the right upper cabinet goes passed the corner, where the skinny base cabinet ends, that throws off the eye\u2018s need for symmetry as well. Even when I look at that last photo that is a cropped view looking straight at the range, I don\u2019t notice the symmetry being off 1.5\u201d. You need to remember that you will see the kitchen as a complete room. What you are looking for is overall balance.  I believe you have that and your kitchen looks beautiful! Now, having that left upper made smaller would be a big mistake in my opinion. Having it not ending in line with the base would jump out more as a mistake to me.  Like you said it makes it awkward where to end the backsplash.", "images": []}}

title: Heat and Drought Tolerant Roses | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "seasiderooftop", "author_name": "seasiderooftop", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/seasiderooftop", "date": "2022-03-02", "text": "Hi everyone,Rather than continue to derail other threads I am creating this one to compile information about heat and drought-tolerant roses.Please don't hesitate to share your best performing roses in high heat, low rainfall areas, or any links to online resources that have listings for such roses.To get things started I will leave some links here.@raingreen 's comments about his experiments in Southern California:https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6235556/it-s-all-tina-marie#n=40Robert Mattock's list of drought tolerant roses in the \"Ibiza rose trials\":http://www.robertmattockroses.com/ibiza.htmOlivier Filippi's list (No way to link to the list directly but search for \"Rosa\" in the searchbox on the upper right side of this page):https://www.jardin-sec.com/jardin-sec_web/fr/Database.awpThe San Jose Heritage Rose garden put together a document on drought tolerant roses in 2014, see their extensive list at the end of this pdf:https://documents.pub/document/drought-tolerant-roses-san-jose-heritage-rose-tolerant-rosespdf-drought-tolerant.htmlIf you know of other resources please add them here!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dcrd", "author_name": "mustbnuts zone 9 sunset 9", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dcrd", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "I grow about half (if not more) of my roses in pots and the others in the ground.  All are on own root except for one.  We get (as I always say), hotter than Hades here in the summer.  We are typically over 100 F from June (sometimes May), until October.  Last summer we got to 116 F again.  It is misery. I use BIG pots for my roses.  They have them at Sam's Club this time of year.  They are at least 22 inches in diameter and are resin pots.  They are much thicker than \"regular\" plastic ones and help to protect the roots from the heat and sun.  I have them on caddies with wheels that will hold over 100 lbs.  Great as they get very heavy between the potting mix, rose and the water.  I also have them on drip and water them daily during the summer for one minute each day.  I also have them in morning sun and afternoon shade from about 3 PM or so.  I don't really feed them from about the end of May until at least the middle of September.  It is too hot and they are just trying to survive.  I want them to survive and not waste energy trying to grow flowers when it is that hot. Now, that being said, the best ones for my pots has been my NOID (no ID) which is a rose I grew from one of Roseseek's seeds--that name is what I call it--it does have an \"official\" name of initials of its parental units--no ID is easier for me.  Others include Peppermint Parfait--a wonderful Ralph Moore rose.  It is first to bloom this year (Already! A month early!).  Minnie Mouse is another great rose that does very, very well.  Violet Hour does great and is gorgeous!  Ah, too early in the morning to think of what else I have out there....I have several \"experiments\" this year. My other roses are on their own in the ground.  I find hybrid perpetuals tend to do well for me on their own root.  Probably my star rose is Vick's Caprice.  Portland from Glendora has done well.  Also Alice Hamilton (I love this rose!).  They are all on drip. Others that do well for me are Ralph Moore's Sequoia Gold, and Halo Sweetie.  A Burling rose Flamingo Dancer is an all star rose as well. For DA roses--Munstead Wood, Pretty Jessica, Mary Magdalene, Princess Alexandra of Kent and Jubilee Celebration do OK.  I have been slowly getting rid of my DA roses as they just are not wild about the heat here.  Probably the best for heat is Pretty Jessica (if you can still find her) and Mary Magdalene (if you can still find her). I just moved Jubilee to a different location where she will get full sun all day, so we shall see how she does.  I am keeping my fingers crossed. My roses that are in the ground are all on drip.  I have water restrictions where I live and can only (during the summer) water 2 or 3 days a week and only during certain hours.  For about half of the year, I can only water one day a week.  Mother Nature does the rest of the watering (and she hasn't been around much over the past several years during winter and is not around at all from May through October).  I am thinking of putting up sunscreen over my roses that get full sun during the day and see if that helps.  I think the homeowners association will probably complain as well as my neighbors, so the jury is out as to whether or not I do this in the front and side yards.  People in Tucson do this with their roses (which many are in pots due to soil, etc., there). Hope that helps!", "images": []}}

More on using a tell: Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source \u2013 photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water \u2013 so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16\u201d (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48\u201d (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. title: Démolir un mur porteur dans le cadre de travaux de rénovation | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "builder-pfvwfr-pf~631388753", "author_name": "Builder", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/general-contractors/builder-pfvwfr-pf~631388753", "date": "2022-03-02", "text": "Travaux de d\u00e9molition avant r\u00e9novation d'un bien ou d\u00e9molition d'un mur porteur Vous souhaitez gagner en place ou en luminosit\u00e9 ? Ouvrir votre cuisine sur votre salon ? Cr\u00e9er un nouvel espace ? Il vous faudra alors certainement casser un mur. R\u00e9aliser des travaux de d\u00e9molition avant r\u00e9novation d\u2019un bien peut n\u00e9cessiter de se faire accompagner par un professionnel, notamment si le mur est porteur. Vous trouverez toutes les informations utiles dans cet article pour r\u00e9aliser parfaitement vos travaux de r\u00e9novation avec d\u00e9molition.  Les raisons de vouloir abattre une cloison ou un mur porteur C\u2019est d\u00e9cid\u00e9, vous souhaitez abattre une cloison. Vous avez r\u00e9fl\u00e9chi mille fois et y trouvez finalement que des bonnes raisons. En effet, casser un mur apporte de nombreux avantages : - Obtenir un espace plus grand, plus ouvert ;- Gagner en luminosit\u00e9 ;- Agencer son espace diff\u00e9remment pour l\u2019optimiser ;- Rendre sa circulation plus ais\u00e9e ;- Changer la disposition des pi\u00e8ces ;- Ouvrir sur l\u2019ext\u00e9rieur ;- R\u00e9aliser un bar, un comptoir ou un passe-plat ;- Cr\u00e9er une ouverture int\u00e9rieure, un passage de porte. Toutes les raisons sont bonnes pour ouvrir son espace par d\u00e9molition d\u2019une cloison. Retrouvez les r\u00e9alisations faites par Builder pour vous donner des id\u00e9es. Mais il faut \u00eatre vigilant sur le type de cloisons. En effet, si le mur est porteur, cela n\u00e9cessite une prise en charge par un professionnel. Nous y reviendrons. Les types de murs porteurs Les murs porteurs sont de trois sortes : - Murs de soubassement : ils supportent les murs de fa\u00e7ade et les murs de refend ;- Murs de fa\u00e7ades : ce sont les murs donnant sur l\u2019ext\u00e9rieur. Ils soutiennent l\u2019ensemble du b\u00e2ti (maison ou immeuble pour un appartement) ;- Murs de refend : ce sont les murs int\u00e9rieurs permettant de stabiliser le b\u00e2ti et de s\u00e9parer les pi\u00e8ces. Reconna\u00eetre un mur porteur avant de le d\u00e9molir   Vous pouvez, seul, avoir une premi\u00e8re id\u00e9e pour d\u00e9terminer si le mur que vous souhaitez abattre est porteur ou non. Tout d\u2019abord, frappez dessus (comme vous toquez \u00e0 une porte). Si le bruit est sourd, il peut s\u2019agir d\u2019un mur porteur. Mais le mat\u00e9riau utilis\u00e9 peut se r\u00e9v\u00e9ler trompeur. Alors ne vous contentez pas de cela pour reconna\u00eetre un mur porteur d\u2019une simple cloison. V\u00e9rifiez si ce mur soutient une poutre, une charpente, un sol ou encore un autre mur. Il y a de grandes chances dans ce cas qu\u2019il soit porteur. Son \u00e9paisseur est aussi parlante. Si la cloison fait au moins une quinzaine de centim\u00e8tres, le mur est surement porteur. Enfin, vous pouvez tout simplement v\u00e9rifier sur le plan du b\u00e2ti si vous l\u2019avez. Le mur porteur est g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement mis en exergue par un trait plus \u00e9pais que les cloisons simples. Et sinon, pour \u00eatre totalement s\u00fbr de vous, faites appel \u00e0 un professionnel comme un architecte d\u2019int\u00e9rieur. Travaux de d\u00e9molition pour r\u00e9nover un bien   Si vous avez besoin d\u2019effectuer des travaux importants pour r\u00e9nover votre bien, vous pouvez le faire seul. Cependant, cela n\u00e9cessite une certaine ma\u00eetrise de plusieurs aspects : - D\u00e9molition de cloisons (techniques, s\u00e9curit\u00e9) ;- \u00c9lectricit\u00e9 ;- Plomberie ;- Pl\u00e2trerie ;- Rattrapage et pose de sols. L\u2019id\u00e9al est de faire appel \u00e0 des professionnels de la r\u00e9novation qui ont toutes les comp\u00e9tences pour votre besoin. Chez Builder, tous les corps de m\u00e9tiers sont repr\u00e9sent\u00e9s et permettent d\u2019avoir une expertise parfaite dans la r\u00e9alisation des travaux. Ils savent orienter vers les comp\u00e9tences n\u00e9cessaires notamment en mati\u00e8re de conception de projet et analyse de mur porteur. Les \u00e9tapes de d\u00e9molition d\u2019un mur porteur Si dans vos travaux de d\u00e9molition avant r\u00e9novation de votre bien se trouve un mur porteur, il est alors n\u00e9cessaire de suivre plusieurs \u00e9tapes. Vous devez forc\u00e9ment \u00eatre accompagn\u00e9 dans ce projet. En voici donc les diff\u00e9rentes phases : - \u00c9tudier le projet avec un architecte d'int\u00e9rieur ;- R\u00e9aliser une \u00e9tude aupr\u00e8s d\u2019un BET (Bureau d\u2019\u00c9tudes Techniques) ;- Faire appel \u00e0 une entreprise sp\u00e9cialis\u00e9e en d\u00e9molition de murs porteurs. Ensuite, l\u2019entreprise de r\u00e9novation posera des \u00e9tais puis une poutre IPN avant de percer le mur porteur. Ensuite, une fois le tout r\u00e9alis\u00e9, ils pourront retirer les \u00e9tais puis r\u00e9aliser les travaux de finition (reprise des sols et des plafonds, peinture, pose de sols\u2026). Faire appel \u00e0 un architecte d\u2019int\u00e9rieur Au-del\u00e0 de la n\u00e9cessit\u00e9 pour la d\u00e9molition d\u2019un mur porteur, faire appel \u00e0 un architecte d\u2019int\u00e9rieur permet de se projeter plus facilement dans son futur nouvel espace. Il va concevoir et r\u00e9aliser un int\u00e9rieur unique, \u00e0 votre go\u00fbt, optimis\u00e9 et fonctionnel en misant sur les volumes, la lumi\u00e8re, les mat\u00e9riaux, le mobilier... Il va \u00e9galement prendre en compte les contraintes techniques, r\u00e9glementaires et budg\u00e9taires de votre projet. Dans la plupart des cas, l\u2019architecte d\u2019int\u00e9rieur vous livre plusieurs propositions afin de pouvoir choisir selon diff\u00e9rentes solutions d\u2019am\u00e9nagement. Bien entendu, il \u00e9tudie la faisabilit\u00e9 du projet. Ensuite, il conseille sur le choix des mat\u00e9riaux, des \u00e9quipements, voire de la d\u00e9coration. Enfin, il coordonne votre projet pendant la r\u00e9novation de votre bien. Par ailleurs, l\u2019architecte s\u2019occupe de g\u00e9rer toutes les d\u00e9marches administratives (permis de construire, demande pr\u00e9alable de travaux, autorisation du syndic de copropri\u00e9t\u00e9\u2026).   La n\u00e9cessit\u00e9 du Bureau d\u2019\u00e9tudes pour casser un mur porteur Si dans votre projet de d\u00e9molition avant r\u00e9novation vous devez abattre un mur porteur, l\u2019architecte d\u2019int\u00e9rieur se mettra en relation avec un bureau d\u2019\u00e9tudes structure. Celui-ci est compos\u00e9 d\u2019ing\u00e9nieurs structure qui vont v\u00e9rifier la faisabilit\u00e9 du projet de d\u00e9molition dans un premier temps. Ensuite, ils vont d\u00e9terminer la m\u00e9thode \u00e0 utiliser : type d\u2019\u00e9l\u00e9ments, dimensions\u2026 Cette \u00e9tape est obligatoire pour abattre un mur porteur. L\u2019\u00e9vacuation des d\u00e9chets D\u00e9molir un mur, porteur ou non, et m\u00eame r\u00e9aliser des travaux de r\u00e9novation engendrent de nombreux d\u00e9chets. Il en existe 3 types : - D\u00e9chets inertes : gravats de b\u00e9tons, briques, parpaings, carrelage, tuiles, verre...- D\u00e9chets non dangereux : plastiques, cartons, bois, plinthes, ferraille, moquette, lino, tuyaux en PVC...- D\u00e9chets dangereux : amiante, plomb (dans la peinture notamment), solvants, cartouches de mastic... Pour les deux premiers (d\u00e9chets inertes et d\u00e9chets non dangereux), vous pouvez vous en charger vous-m\u00eame en d\u00e9chargeant directement vos gravats en d\u00e9ch\u00e8terie. Cependant, pour les d\u00e9chets dangereux, vous devez faire appel \u00e0 un professionnel. Pour \u00e9vacuer vos d\u00e9chets, plusieurs solutions s\u2019offrent \u00e0 vous : - Sac \u00e0 gravats : pour les d\u00e9chets peu volumineux. Vous en trouvez de plusieurs tailles et de diff\u00e9rentes mati\u00e8res selon votre besoin.- Benne : elle permet d\u2019\u00e9vacuer les d\u00e9chets encombrants. En cas d\u2019\u00e9vacuation en pleine rue, il faut anticiper de demander une autorisation \u00e0 la mairie de votre commune.- Aspirateur \u00e0 gravats : il finalise le d\u00e9blaiement des d\u00e9chets.   R\u00e9aliser des travaux de r\u00e9novation est un projet \u00e0 ne pas prendre \u00e0 la l\u00e9g\u00e8re. L\u2019id\u00e9al est donc de se faire accompagner par des professionnels du batiment et de bien pr\u00e9parer et concevoir en amont l\u2019architecture int\u00e9rieure \u00e0 toutes les \u00e9tapes pour b\u00e9n\u00e9ficier d\u2019une solution cl\u00e9 en main et sur-mesure. title: Did you ever have a midnight wing it success? | Houzz Forum

Wanna share some successes? The other day, I started making a standard egg bake (like a crustless quiche) at 11 p.m.  I don't need to be awake for that.  Broccolini, spring onion, chop chop chop, oil dish, eggs and milk/cream, flavorings, cheese I'd grated earlier on top, bake.  No thought involved. But then I thought, what about the banana bread.  I keep having leftover, overripe bananas that never get made into banana bread, even though I'd gotten blueberries for the purpose (I like blueberries and pistachios in banana bread).  I came to the conclusion that the bananas had gone to rot because I really didn't want to make banana bread!  But I again had bananas, and the blueberries would rot too if I didn't use them.  I'd made that good banana custard pie.  Why not do one egg bake style, I thought, and bake it with the broccoli-onion? Blueberries--and a sprinkling of whole (whole!) pistachios in the bottom of a pie plate, Mashed bananas in a light custard (turned out a bit watery since there was nothing to absorb the water from the milk and I didn't bother opening more cream).  I added some flavors, but didn't remember what they were until I tasted it the next day.  For sure cloves and Cointreau.  I think the rest comes from the graham crackers.  The remainder of the box from when I was making the roll out demo was sitting there and I was thinking the custard needed a topping and I didn't want to bother with a crumble.  So I just crushed three of these overly sweet, dry as the Mojave \"Honey Maids\" in my hands over the dish to make scattered crumbs, and they added a lot of sweet and a little honey flavor while making an acceptable looking top.  (And I gave away the rest of the box the next day.) This is not what I'd have made if I'd been fully awake, but it's surprisingly, pretty good. :)  It would have  been very good if the pistachios were chopped, the cream had been used and the topping had be a proper oat crumble with some dried blueberries and pistachios in it. title: Potted Lemon tree in trouble | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-19453286", "author_name": "Zhanna Campbell", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-19453286", "date": "2022-03-02", "text": "Hello, I bought an orange and a lemon trees, about 1.5m each. Both have been repotted, living indoors - winter here in Canada. Orange is doing really well. Lemon isn't. I've changed the soil to make it more easy to drain, pots are standing on supports allowing for water to drain freely and air the bottom of the pot. But leaves are becoming yellow, and roll, some got really soft, although top of the tree is still green. But weirdest thing happens to the many blooms it had when I bought it. Most of them don't open, don't fall, they kind of..petrify on the tree, unopen petals encapsulating the flower in rubber-like shells. The ones which open are sickly too. When I measure moisture, it's very dry at the ball of the root and very wet on the outside, I have a moisture meter. I've read everything I could find, and as I mentioned before, I changed the potting mix etc but still my tree seems to be overwatered and underwatered at the same time. Plus, whatever is happening to the flowers and buds. I'd very much appreciate your thoughts and ideas. I have theoretical knowledge but 0 experience. Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_name": "bonsai_citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "date": "2022-03-05", "text": "When you repotted your tree, did you remove the old medium from the roots or just leave the medium in place? If you left the medium in place, then you wind up with two different drainage patterns for your well draining mix and the original soil. Not a good situation. I would repot the tree, remove the old medium, and place the tree in new. Then submerge the pot so that the whole rootball gets soaked, or conversely run a hose through it until no more bubbles appear. Also, I would beware my moisture meter. Different moisture meters are calibrated in different soils, therefore they can be off if you're using them in a soil different than they were made for. If you want to use the moisture meter you need to \"calibrate\" it for yourself by figuring out what it reads as dry and wet for your soil. Use a chopstick or a wood skewer stuck down into the soil and feel the wood. Then put your meter in the soil and see what it reads. If the stick is wet, then whatever the meter is reading is \"wet\" if dry, then the meter is reading \"dry\". Use this to get a feel for when to water.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "therickestrick", "author_name": "TheRickestRick", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/therickestrick", "date": "2022-03-03", "text": "Hello, i am typically a cannabis grower and these little guys sproated up in one of my pots about 3 weeks ago    so i decided to replant it and see what it was. i believe i have successfully identified it as a cucumber but just want to check before i keep it growing.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5e92416d02201838_0525-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2b2246210220183b_0527-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "highcolddesert", "author_name": "HighColdDesert", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/highcolddesert", "date": "2022-03-04", "text": "I'm no expert at telling the various cucurbits apart at this stage, but it is definitely a cucurbit. Personally I can't guess accurately at this stage if it's cucumber, melon or squash. Are you using homemade compost? One tip is that cucumbers we buy generally have immature seeds and are less likely to volunteer from the compost (because fully ripe cucumbers get sour and seedy and less good to eat). Melons and winter squash we buy and eat have ripe seeds which are very good at volunteering in compost. If a gardener lets  cucumbers stay on the vine too long, their seeds are viable. Many people online strongly recommend against growing on seeds that grow from garden vegetables, with an extreme fear that they might be from hybrids or cross-pollinations. But most cucurbits except Cucurbita pepo are fine. I've done it, and the science/logic is fine. They won't have the special properties the hybrid was bred for, but they will produce edible and maybe delicious melons, cukes, winter squash, because most of these have one general type per species, so cross pollination within the species will still produce plants producing that general type. For example a seed from a cantaloupe/muskmelon will surely produce a cantaloupe/muskmelon, and it will likely be a yummy one if it gets time to ripen, but it won't have the special disease resistant or other properties of the mother plant the seed came from. Same with cucumbers and C. maxima winter squash. C. pepo species is problematic because zucchini, spaghetti squash, delicata, acorn squash, and bitter toxic ornamental gourds are all in this species, so crosses may actually be weird or unusable, and if bitter, then they're toxic.", "images": []}}

title: The $%^& Parfait (semi-update) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bbstxx", "author_name": "bbstx", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bbstxx", "date": "2022-03-03", "text": "Some time ago, I posted about a parfait I\u2019m making for tomorrow\u2019s cookbook club luncheon.  https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6236757/how-far-ahead-can-this-parfait-be-made#n=17  My question was how far ahead can I make this.  My answer is \u201dnot far enough.\u201d This morning I made the crumble.  It is oats (rolled and steel-cut), pecans, and pumpkin seeds.  All of that is folded into beaten egg whites flavored with cayenne, ground fennel, sugar, and salt.  Add to that neutral oil and Worcestershire sauce. The instructions say to whip the egg whites until foamy then add all the other ingredients and beat until stiff peaks form.  [may I yell here?]  YOU CANNOT DO THAT!! Stiff peaks will not form after you add the oil.  I read the instructions until I was blue.  Having said that, the crumble was not as weird as I thought it was going to be.  It is actually pretty tasty. Not wanting to get ahead of myself, I waited until mid-afternoon to start on the elements of the parfait.  The first layer is a sort of blueberry jam.  It went well, but not quickly.  I think it would have been better without the lime zest.  Then it had to chill for an hour and a half. The next step was the buttermilk panna cotta.  The cookbook author admonishes you to strain the mixture because it will curdle.  Nope.  No curdling.  I strained it, nevertheless.  It is very thin.  I cannot do the lime curd layer until the panna cotta has set up.  I\u2019m hoping the panna cotta sets up.  The gelatin to liquid ratios seem to be okay compared to other recipes I found.  It is 1/2 envelope of gelatin (I weighed it to get exactly half) to 3/4 cup cream and 1 2/3 cup buttermilk. I\u2019m tired.  I think i have a disaster on my hands.  I\u2019m going to make the lime curd in the morning so that the panna cotta has sufficient time to set up.  If it doesn\u2019t set up, I\u2019ll serve the lime curd and whipped cream on the side and call it \u201ddeconstructed parfait.\u201d  \ud83d\ude09 @plllog, remember how you were concerned about the parfaits taking up odors in the fridge and I told you I never cooked anything stinky?  Guess what I did today?  Boiled eggs!  OMG.  I had to double bag them to control the smell.  I did discover a simple way to cover the parfaits\u2026cookie sheet turned over on them! Watch this space for tomorrow\u2019s installment of \u201dHow the Kitchen Turns.\u201d", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bbstxx", "author_name": "bbstx", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bbstxx", "date": "2022-03-03", "text": "The parfait was declared \u201dthe best dessert we\u2019ve had since the beginning of the club.\u201d \ud83e\udd47  Watch me strut!  The crumble was a big big hit.  It was sweet with a little spicy back note. I think the recipe could have been better written.  I think some elements were unnecessarily fiddly. We got the answers to some questions posed in the first thread: - First and foremost, you cannot make this dessert in one day.  I certainly could not have made it the morning of the luncheon, especially considereing how long it took the panna cotta to set up (lacking a walk-in freezer\u2026very funny @lisaam!) - I do not believe you can make each element ahead of time and then layer everything.  Well, you can, but the layers won\u2019t be nice and even.  They set up.  In fact, if you look at my picture above, you will notice that the lime curd layer was not perfectly flat on top. title: Flooring Direction? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mkille", "author_name": "mkille", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mkille", "date": "2022-03-04", "text": "How did you decide what \"direction\" to lay flooring in your house? I asked my flooring company but they said it's really just personal preference. If I lay it one way it would run the same direction as the longest length of the house (and the flow of how we move most often) and one hallway, but would be perpendicular to the front door and another hallway. And if I run it the other way it would be perpendicular on one hallway but run with the flow of when you walk in the front door. Basically, either configuration has pros/cons so I'm wondering....is there a \"rule of thumb\" that designers usually recommend?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kempek01", "author_name": "kempek01", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kempek01", "date": "2022-03-04", "text": "A floor plan would help us provide input. If the flooring is all connected, then you may have to  make a compromise in the \"flow\" somewhere, or you find a place where you can logically change directions. The floor joists also help determine direction. Hardwood flooring is typically laid perpendicular to the joists.  I don't think LVP tile has that restriction, but you would want to consult your flooring expert. By the way, my hardwoods are separated by tile into two areas.  The two areas of hardwood run in different directions.  Doesn't bother me at all.  If they were joined together (and the tile was replaced with wood), I would still have the flooring running in two directions because of the joists (and the flow of the house).  But I am not open concept, so the walls and doorway openings provide a natural place to make the change in direction", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "missindie1", "author_name": "Chessie", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/missindie1", "date": "2022-03-04", "text": "I ran my engineered wood from the front door straight out to back of house.  I turned it at the hallway as that just looked better to me.  The ends were a perfect T%G fit so no transition was needed at all, it looks great.  The main area is not perpendicular to the joists, but that really isn't a problem and would not really become one for many many years, if ever.  (It was sort of \"old school\" to think it had to be done that way - now it is pretty much your preference).", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "southeasthouse", "author_name": "southeasthouse", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/southeasthouse", "date": "2022-03-04", "text": "LOL at these classic Houzz answers - you ask a question about something you like, and people instead answer with what they like. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-2068556725", "author_name": "V", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-2068556725", "date": "2022-03-04", "text": "Hello - I had my house painted while I was out of town, and when I got home saw immediately that the color wasn't what I had picked. Has this ever happened to anyone else? Is it reasonable for me to expect the painter to help make this right, without completely recharging me? I had sent him a photo of the formula before starting and feel like he should have noticed when he painted over the 6 or 7 swatches I had on the wall.", "images": []}

I", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "colette100", "author_name": "Marylee H", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/colette100", "date": "2022-03-05", "text": "Paint has measured colour attributes which paint companies use as a target to ensure consistency from batch to batch. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-939974324", "author_name": "J Dubbs", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-939974324", "date": "2022-03-05", "text": "Heres the situation.. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "g-and-s-floor-service-pfvwus-pf~1829880277", "author_name": "G & S Floor Service", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/flooring-contractors/g-and-s-floor-service-pfvwus-pf~1829880277", "date": "2022-03-05", "text": "Effloresce is what you will need to worry about over concrete floors or below grade installations.  The white powdery substance forming in the joints.  On and above grade is usually not needed, unless otherwise stated.  What did the instructions from the manufacturer state regarding vapor barriers? title: Help/Critique of Kitchen Layout? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mn-lake_life", "author_name": "V On The Lake", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mn-lake_life", "date": "2022-03-05", "text": "Hello Houzz community! It's been great to read through the numerous posts and contributions of so many posters over the years, and now it's time to start some asking! TLDR: Looking for feedback on this kitchen layout! Any constructive input appreciated! Background: Husband and I are very handy and have lots of tools. We both have backgrounds in construction and/or engineering and have undertaken some major construction projects in the past. We own a cabin that we call home year round in Minnesota that has some structural issues, a poor layout, and was last redone in the mid 90s. After searching the housing market in our area for the past several years, we've decided to rebuild in our current location with a target date of summer 2023. We are very restricted with the square footage we can add onto our structure, but we can expand some in certain directions. In all of these plans the lake views are to the south (bottom). We will hire a contractor to build the house with the exception of a few items that we will likely undertake ourselves. One of those items will probably be the kitchen cabinets. I've designed, ordered, and built an IKEA kitchen in a former house around 10 years ago (around 2/3 of the size of this project), and I found the process overall pretty easy. After living with it for around 5 years, I still loved it. The Blum hardware is great, the finishes held up really well for me, and it is really hard to find modern styled anything in the rural area where I live. This is a realistic way for us to get a look we like and build some equity in the process. Caveats: Yes, I know IKEA has been having major supply chain issues in the past 2 years and ordering kitchens is challenging right now. If 16 months from now the situation is not improved, we'll look for either another RTA option or to a local kitchen store. Furthermore the IKEA home design app is not the best, so the iso renderings are not 100% accurate to the current design. I'll order piece by piece through their web interface and have it delivered as I have in the past successfully. Materials: Currently we're planning on IKEA Sektion cabinets - uppers and pantry being Ringhult gloss white, other lowers likely Semihandmade either Walnut or Impression doors/drawer fronts. Counter will likely be a lighter color Cambria installed by a local professional. We will have an open mudroom/entryway that will probably be custom hacked over-fridge IKEA cabs with the Semihandmade fronts and a 15\" bank of cabinets above one one side for extra closed storage. Appliances are another challenge. Thinking Bosch panel front dishwasher, TBD 30\" induction range or dual fuel range, Kitchenaid slim microwave hood (I know), and TBD fridge - I love the look of the white gloss Samsung 4 door Bespoke, but they are hard to get serviced here and have a horrible reputation. Maybe one of Bosch's 4-door models. Design Thought Process: - It's a 2BR + 1 office house, and we're designing for us 2 adults to live here with our dogs. We don't have room for a separate pantry, so we need to have some dry good storage in the kitchen. I do have a detailed plan in mind for a build-out at the end of the island that can house outlets and our dogs' food/water bowls. - I prefer nearly all lowers to be drawers (yay Blum hardware), with the exception being a cabinet in the island with a lift for my stand mixer and a matching one on the other side of the island - The choice on the induction range is based on the house being super energy efficient and a tight build with limited capacity for makeup air - I'd prefer to not have a bunch of combustion byproducts to try to effectively vent all the time. We do still need a hood vent of some sort to handle any accidental smoky conditions or very fragrant foods. We also need a spot for a microwave, and I'd rather not do a drawer model or have it take up space on our counters. Hence, the slim model Kitchenaid micro hood (or maybe Samsung or Whirlpool that also have models available). I can't figure out an alternative solution that would give us a nicer looking hood option other than putting a countertop microwave inside one of the pantry cabinets (not very safe). - I prefer not to have the cooktop or sink in the island space. One reason is to have a larger work area for some specific ethnic foods I make. I also had my sink in the island in my past Ikea kitchen and didn't love eating next to the sink. - We plan on upgrading the corner cabinet lazy suzan to a heavy duty one from Rev-a-shelf vs. the cheapy Ikea one. Unresolved Questions: - I think two of my biggest questions come down to drawer layout. 5-10-15 vs 10-10-10 for the island drawer banks. I don't know if it really matters. I think 10-10-10 looks better, but then the silverware would be in a drawer within a drawer (annoying), and I don't have a lot of options for deeper storage in the kitchen currently. Similarly with the pantry cabinets - how many drawers makes sense for true use as a pantry? Drawer fronts also add cost - maybe I'd consider doing a pull-out in the lower half with interior drawers I can adjust later and doors above? - Should I match the edge of the northernmost pantry cabinet to the edge of the island and increase the pathway between the sink and island more than 42\"? - Also, any brilliant solutions for the microwave situation I haven't thought through yet? Anything else I'm missing?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/026254130223c349_0937-w500-h1111-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6ac25cba0223c34a_0922-w500-h450-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/205260b20223c34a_0923-w500-h288-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a012723b0223c34b_0923-w500-h349-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2022-03-06", "text": "The origins of steampunk go back to the speculative fiction and related illustrative art of the late 19th c. (Jules Verne, HG Wells), and also alternative history/future fictional technologies. The term itself originated in the 1980s but the ideas of such, things looking steampunk/being in fiction, predate this, the show Wild, Wild West (1965), and movie Brazil (1985) The sets and devices of The Time Machine (1960) and 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea (1954) are steampunk. The ideas really have a presence in Japanese literature and movies back to the 1940s. The Arts et Metiers metro station (1994) is steampunk--a thirty year old design, really.  The Waterstone wheel faucet qualifies as steampunk, I think, (retail $5000-6000) and I think this has been around 10 + years because back in the old days of \"Design Around  . . . .\" this was used in a steampunk round of that activity on the old GW and that had to be ten years ago anyway, because I lived in a different house.  So I don't really think that it is a \"trend\" or a \"fad\" as much as it is an alternative design/literature philosophy that has paralleled more mainstream design for at least a couple decades (much like the goth movement and other punk movements) that occasionally intersects with more mainstream design, but never really caught the fancy of the larger public particularly in residential settings.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ce8271530224b981_3958-w240-h176-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/186201390224ba19_4105-w240-h358-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

main_question: {"author_id": "seasiderooftop", "author_name": "seasiderooftop", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/seasiderooftop", "date": "2022-03-06", "text": "Hi everyone,Two years ago I went to see a dermatologist. She mentioned selenium supplements, saying they were great antioxidants and could help the skin deal with UV exposure. She also mentioned that many studies had proved the efficacy of selenium enrichment in wheat to increase the heat and sun tolerance of the crops.Well, somehow that conversation took two years to get processed through my brain and I'm only reaching the obvious question now. Why not try selenium to help my container plants handle our insane heat ? I'm in zone 11, Malta. The summers here are basically two months of nonstop sweltering heat, with several weeks above 40\u00b0c.The problem is, how to find an adequate selenium source? I can't find any readily available selenium fertilizer. The only ones I see are bulk for industrial agriculture.Since the plants only require a very tiny amount I am thinking of just breaking up a tablet of my own selenium supplement and diluting bits of it in the watering can once a month.I checked Mulder's Chart and it doesn't look like the selenium would interfere with the other minerals.Has anyone tried supplementing their plants with selenium?Do you know of any fertilizers that specifically include selenium and are available for hobby gardeners?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "seasiderooftop", "author_name": "seasiderooftop", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/seasiderooftop", "date": "2022-03-08", "text": "Just leaving an update here in case it can be useful to anyone else looking to add selenium. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~125880644", "author_name": "Diana Bier Interiors, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~125880644", "date": "2022-03-06", "text": "What you're asking is difficult to impossible to answer.  Paint color on the walls should be the last item that you choose, after all the permanent fixtures are in.  I know builders want to paint first, but that makes it frustrating to homeowners.  Color changes with the light, and is influenced by everything else in the room.  When we built our home, we had everything painted white.  If we wanted to paint the walls a different color at a later date, we did that ourselves and had time to consider what the best color would be. Gray Screen is in the blue/green color family, so it makes sense that it tends to look cooler than Repose Gray which is in the yellow color family. (Usually the supplies are in the ceiling and to get the heat to go down to the floor is contrary to thermal dynamics).  Forced air systems are usually very cost effective and gives the option for air conditioning, so I would use that for the majority of the house and use radiant in floor hot water heat with an electric boiler for the basement. (It will also give you a drier basement, especially if you open the A/C vents in the summer).", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "davidpilati", "author_name": "David Cary", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/davidpilati", "date": "2022-03-06", "text": "Julie - There really isn't that much temperature stratification to worry about. Especially if you are talking about opening a/c vents? How does that correlate to radiant heat? If radiant were to leak, that would be better under basement slab - I suppose that is one reason. The diminished need for a/c in a basement would be another.  Concrete slab is the cheapest way to do radiant is another reason. If you insulate the basement well (and you should), then the heat load is pretty low (few windows, conditioned space above, minimal air leakage). title: Do I need make-up air in the Northern Virginia area. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-101012217", "author_name": "Shevas", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-101012217", "date": "2022-03-07", "text": "We want to install a 36 inch NXR Pro cooktop to replace our existing cooktop with a downdraft. So we are getting rid of the downdraft and would like to install a powerful 1000 CFM range hood made by NXR Pro. The space is not tight by any means and we have very high ceilings on the whole level. The living level is roughly about 2000 square feet of space", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-101012217", "author_name": "Shevas", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-101012217", "date": "2022-03-07", "text": "Here's what the code for Virginia says: M1503.4 Makeup Air RequiredExhaust hood systems capable of exhausting more than 400 cubic feet per minute (0.19 m3/s) shall be provided with makeup air at a rate approximately equal to the exhaust air rate in excess of 400 cubic feet per minute (0.19 m3/s). Such makeup air systems shall be equipped with a means of closure and shall be automatically controlled to start and operate simultaneously with the exhaust system.Exception: Intentional openings for makeup air are not required for kitchen exhaust systems capable of exhausting not greater than 600 cubic feet per minute (0.28 m3/s) provided that one of the following conditions is met:", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2022-03-07", "text": "Beyond the safety issues expressed in the code, no air leaves the kitchen via the hood system that isn't replaced somehow.  One can't just drain the house volume of air.  Further, if the hood system has to lower the house pressure to get enough air from house leakage, the hood air flow rate will be degraded, and stuff in the walls may find its way into the living areas. If you search this forum for \"MUA\" you will find various ideas and conditions for adopting them.  Depending on the type of combustion appliances in your house that are within the \"air barrier,\" you may need a blower-driven MUA path (active MUA) or a large duct (passive MUA).  Both will need some form of heating and filtering. You may notice that active vs. passive is not explicitly called out in the code text listed above, nor is there an explicit demand for a particular pressure balance.  Once review of the material here leads you to feel comfortable with the issues, you might want to discuss your MUA system plan with your local code enforcement to ensure that you are both on the same page. Alternatively, finding an informed HVAC contractor may be sufficient.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "hzdeleted-70038741", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-70038741", "date": "2022-03-07", "text": "Yes, it is REQUIRED.", "images": []}}

title: Sometimes the pan really does matter | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "plllog", "author_name": "plllog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/plllog", "date": "2022-03-08", "text": "I grew up with cornpone rather than cornbread.  Less risen, more sour and a bit greasy.  Mother used to make it in the classic corn shaped molds, but those shed too much iron for me, and gave me a tummy ache when I was a kid, but making proper camp cornpone (but in a pan rather than on a shovel or hoe) was just right.  It's almost as good made on the stove in an ordinary skillet.  Sweet cornbread, to me, is cake, not a proper quickbread.  I had a hard time finding a recipe I truly liked until Arley's posts about the Bernard Clayton recipe.  But that recipe requires a heated vessel of a particular size, which I could only sort of approximate (it being too hot for my glass and stoneware pans).  I still managed to make a better cornbread than I had with other recipes.  ETA:  Lots of cornbread recipes here along with Arley's recipe which I use. Given how good the recipe was, I decided I could do with a \"cornbread pan\".  That is, a 9x9\" that would be happy enough at 450\u00b0 F.  This Nordic Ware one is heavy plain aluminum with rolled edges and even a cover.  Perfect!  But then there was no occasion for cornbread, and I didn't need it for other stuff, and I finally put it away in the cabinet of rarely used oddities. Not so long later, the farm I order my produce from offered \"red\" cornmeal.  I always like their interesting and different offerings, so I bought a little bag.  And left the canister on the counter so I wouldn't forget it.  What was unavailable for my order was the rolls I had wanted because I was too busy to bake bread.  Perfect!  Red cornbread!  In the \"cornbread pan\".  It was happy as the proverbial clam in the oven while I finished up my cooking.  I didn't expect how loud the batter would be! The red  corn is nice and bakes up light, but is a little short of corn flavor and could have used a little more salt, or even (surprisingly) sugar, or honey.  But it's excellent with a dab of butter and a drop of jam.  The pan and its cover are absolutely perfect!  Except when my guest said she was going to help herself to a piece of cake and I said, \"Sure, but it's cornbread.\"  She passed. :)  It does look like cake in the pan...", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/cd6263f50226c07d_6816-w500-h341-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

This is a good-sized challenge. My suggestion is to create a product that falls somewhere between an opaque paint and a perfectly transparent stain. Start with some scrap wood that is similar in color to your ceiling. (Or, plan to sand your new coating off of any area of the ceiling that you coat but don\u2019t like.) It\u2019s likely impossible to altogether hide the red and orange tones without hiding most of the original grain pattern, however, I wouldn\u2019t want to discourage you from trying. If you have access to General Finishes or to SamaN stains, I encourage you to experiment with some of their water-based stains. Scuff sand the surface of your ceiling and before you brush on the stain. (These products are unique in that they allow you to coat a surface that has already been stained/sealed.) Start with a color of your choice as well as some of their \u201cnatural\u201d or untinted stain. Intermix the color and the uncolored stain until you come up with a sufficient level of translucency that will cover your objectionable tones without altogether obscuring the grain. Whether or not you obscure the grain, you might choose to add a second layer of stain that\u2019s more translucent and slightly darker. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gina-gionta", "author_name": "Gina G", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gina-gionta", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "We finished the floors and we love how they turned out! I didn\u2019t really have any issues with blotchiness or anything like that. Thank you everyone for the advice before we started the finish. This is what we ended up going with: 2 coats of Bona Nordic Seal. Used only a T bar, not a roller because I felt that a roller was more likely to have too many start and stop marks because of the white pigment. I just made sure to keep even pressure on the Tbar and not too thick of a coat, but we definitely kept within the coverage rate stated on the bottle. We did both coats on Saturday and then allowed it to dry overnight. Honestly even after the 1st coat of Nordic seal, it didn\u2019t look blotchy at all. But I\u2019m still glad we went with 2 coats. Sunday we applied the first coat of Bona Traffic HD Extra Matte. Let that dry about 4 hours and then used the square buff with 220 over all of the areas quickly so that we didn\u2019t take up too much finish. Cleaned up all of the dust and made sure there was no debris anywhere. We applied the final coat of Traffic HD and are now waiting at least 3 days for furniture to move upstairs. For the Traffic HD, we actually used both a Tbar and roller so we could have two areas being finished at the same time. title: Seedling lighting recommendations | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-107419837", "author_name": "H P Zone 6", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-107419837", "date": "2022-03-10", "text": "what lighting do seedlings require when grown inside for hardening off to go outside? what brands have you tried? what are the technical requirements of the lights and their vicinty to seedlings? please try to reccomend solutions that are economical. i realize that there are lights marketed for this purpose but what \u201doff-label\u201d if you will, lights could be used in leu? tganks in advance", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2022-03-10", "text": "Just a note - depending on your situation, fluorescent lights can be useful, compared with LEDs. I do my winter starts in an unheated converted garage, in which the temperatures can get down into the 40sF. Fluorescent lights provide some heat, so I can throw a tarp or blanket over the whole setup, and keep things nice and warm. No heating mats or tape needed. Adjusting the coverage keeps the temperature under the covers to 70-80F, which the starts love. Fluorescent shop light fixtures are getting a little hard to get, and  I now have an upper level of LEDs as well, but the fluorescents are the ones that keep everyone warm. As noted, T8 \"daylight\" bulbs are good, where the top foliage should be an inch or so away from the lights. The light will be too dim if farther away. As noted, risers are handy for height adjustment as the seedlings grow. Just blocks of wood will do the trick. I keep a stack of 1x4s and 2x4s nearby. I would not bother with expensive grow-light bulbs or horticultural fixtures. Those might be optimal for maturing plants, but they're overkill for seedlings. Nothing special about lighting requirements for hardening off.", "images": []}}

I have carrier heat pump unit that was showing fault \"Code 47 No 230V to Unit\" and the unit was not working.   As anyone would do, I flipped the breaker once on/off to see if that would solve the issue.  So when I came back up to check on the thermo, to my surprised, the unit was completely blank, no power, no light, no nothing!  as if it was \"fried\".  Later, with the power on, I tested the disconnect boxes and had power going in and out of them (indoor and outdoor disconnect boxes). With the outdoor unit, I also removed the access panel and tested the contact by pushing it in .. when I push it in, I hear a short start-up buzzing sound that goes away in 1-3 sec.  It sounds like it wants to start, but it'snot getting sufficient power (capacitor issues?). So, seems like I have 2 issues that may or may not be related. 1- Thermo is completely gone 2- No power or not enough power at the unit This is the extent of my testing and knowledge.  What is the next step of troubleshooting here?  Can I purchase a generic thermostat to see if at least the thermo issue is resolved? Any help is appreciated. Thanks.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "abygail-h", "author_name": "Abygail H.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/abygail-h", "date": "2022-03-10", "text": "Hi,My Fittonia was desperately in need of water so I gave it some. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "floral-uk", "author_name": "floral_uk z.8/9 SW UK", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/floral-uk", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": "Can you post a picture?", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "abygail-hooten", "author_name": "Abygail H", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/abygail-hooten", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": "", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a5129e68022b332c_8320-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg"]}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "ken-adrian", "author_name": "ken_adrian Adrian MI cold Z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ken-adrian", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": "it was stressed .. you watered it ... did NOT give it time to recover  ... so you watered it more ... frankly.. if your pot drains... i cant figure how you overwatered it ... and then.. you panicked.. and repotted an already stressed plant ... diagnosis ... your plant is stressed ... leave it alone .. presuming you used dampened media .. and watered it in properly ... then just leave it alone for a week or two ... too much love can be worse than not enough ... be patient .. ken ps:  its stressed not hungry.. fert is not a response to stress ...", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "abygail-hooten", "author_name": "Abygail H", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/abygail-hooten", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": "Thank you for your advise! Is it wise to let the plant stand on the pebble tray? I went for this option because I also noticed that the air in my house is very dry lately.", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": "I can give you most of the information you'll need to reason through what's happening, but given what we know at this point, it will be up to you to decide what the likely cause of the wilting is. Plants in containers are always \"stressed\" because container gardening is inherently stressful to plants; too, stress comes in many forms and directions, and to varying degrees. \"Stress\" simply means the plant is growing under the influence of  imperfect cultural conditions, or, perhaps more accurately, stress occurs when the plant is growing at or near the limits of what it is genetically programmed to tolerate. The key issue isn't whether or not a plant is stressed; rather, the questions are to what degree it's stressed and what is the CAUSE of the stress. If, when your plant first started wilting, you could still detect moisture in the soil with a \"tell\" or a finger, it's a pretty sure bet the cause wasn't under-watering. If a plant wilts while the soil is moist, it's usually one of three issues, 1) there is an excessive amount of water in the grow medium, which limits the root system's oxygen supply which in turn limits the plant's ability to efficiently take up and move water to all of its parts, or 2) a high level of dissolved solids (salts) have accumulated in the grow medium and soil solution. This can nullify the plant's ability to move water through its cells' permeable membrane (osmosis). The level of dissolved solids can reach levels so high that water stops moving into cells and begins to be pulled out of cells by the same mechanism that curing salt pulls water from the cells of meat like ham/ bacon/ sausage. When this reversal of water occurs, plasmalemma is torn from cell walls as the water moves out and the cell collapses. The scientific name for this disorder is 'plasmolysis', but commonly referred to as fertilizer burn., or 3) The root system is infected by a pathogen which limits its ability to take up water and nutrients dissolved therein. Did you inspect the roots when you repotted? Did they look healthy with white or tan fleshy tips, or did they smell sour, with many black or slimy roots? Often, fungal infections which cause root rot will create conditions such that when you tug on an affected root, the outer covering slides off and leaves behind the root's ventral core (vascular cylinder). Plants that wilt from over-watering usually perk up at night. This is because small openings in leaves (stomata) close during the dark cycle. This limits water loss through these openings, which allows the plant to rebuild its internal water pressure (turgidity) which relieves wilting to some degree. Is it wise to let the plant stand on the pebble tray? A humidity tray can be 'somewhat' helpful in that it slows evaporative water loss from the plant to the air surrounding it, which tends to increase the the plant's internal water pressure (turgidity) which helps to counter the tendency to wilt. Al", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "irika", "author_name": "irika", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/irika", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": "Hi Can somebody tell me when counting kitchen cabinet depth does cabinet door counts?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "buehl", "author_name": "Buehl", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/buehl", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": ">>  If you're asking if the stated depth of a cabinet includes the doors/drawer fronts, the answer is no. Kitchen cabinet depths only account for the cabinet box.  Doors & drawer fronts add about another inch. So, a 24\" deep cabinet is 26\" when counting box + doors/drawer fronts. Knobs/pulls add another 1\" to 2\", depending on your hardware. Counter overhangs extend around 1.5\" beyond the cabinet boxes. >>  If you're asking if you should include doors/drawer fronts when determining the depth of a cabinet, the answer is yes. title: OT - Winter Lingers, Yet Spring Is Near - Musings from Summerland | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rick-sauder", "author_name": "Rideau Rose Lad", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rick-sauder", "date": "2022-03-11", "text": "It has been a very long while since I last posted my garden musings on the Antique Roses Forum.  It is still winter here in the Great White North of the Okanagan Valley.  But I made the trip to the Summerland Ornamental Gardens this morning to see how much snow was still on the rose beds and to do an assessment.  I wrote the bit below for the Ladies on my Rose Team.  I thought perhaps it might fit here as well, particularly for those of you who live in a more northerly climate.  A bit of a break from the incessant trials and tribulations that haunt our news cycles perhaps. Cheers, Rick I returned from the Gardens this morning after spending some time wandering and assessing, both roses and the Garden as a whole.  On the way back I was listening to Sergei Rochmaninof \u2013 \u201cHow Fair This Place\u201d and to Samuel Barber\u2019s \u2013 \u201cThere\u2019s Nae Lark\u201d  Both pieces seemed somewhat serendipitous after my time spent alone in the winter garden. The background to my musings in the Garden was the persistent soughing of the late winter wind through the bare canopy of the great old trees that are the sentinels of the place.  The two symphony pieces picked up on the somber, yet expectant mood of the winter garden.  No folk, no animals, just myself, the dormant plants and patches of persistent snow here and there about.  Grey trees and brown trunks, white patches, coniferous greens, yellow grasses, still a winter palate.  An austere place, a waiting place, an expectant place!  A backdrop of clouds and veils of snow set the scene across the lake in the mountains to the east.  Yet there were small signs of spring if I looked closely enough.  The Witch Hazels are in bloom; Snowdrops, tiny beauties, white and green against the frozen earth, and the first glimpse of shoots of Crocuses are breaking the soil.  No, not spring, still winter, but winter is tired and getting ready to depart.  And then we will greet the spring.   There is a special beauty in the Garden, especially \u201cCanada\u2019s Secret Garden\u201d on a grey day at the end of winter.  The raw beauty of the plantings, devoid of leaf and green; they are stark, yet stalwart and beautiful as they stand against the wind and the sky. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jennifer-hogan285", "author_name": "Jennifer Hogan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jennifer-hogan285", "date": "2022-03-13", "text": "Are you planning on painting the existing trim and cabinets?  Whites often don't play well together, so matching existing is often easier than picking a new white. If you want a light neutral that contrasts with your white you will still want to consider the trim and cabinet colors and the undertones. Your sofa looks violet gray next to your current wall color, so that is going to be a driving force.  Greige (green gray/ green beige) may look a bit dingy with the sofa and taupe (violet gray/ pink beige) may go lilac on your walls next to your flooring. In your case, where you have both the yellow/gray flooring and the violet gray sofa I would start with getting a bunch of neutral color swatches and try to figure out what you like with your sofa and your flooring. It is sometimes easier to find the color family that works best by looking at mid toned colors.  You can then choose a lighter version of the color. Maria Killam lists some examples of colors in different families that may get you started.   She didn't always pick my favorites from each family, but it is a decent variety and will guide you to the right color space..  Her green grey is more of a greige than a green gray in my book, but she doesn't have greige on her color wheel, only green gray and green beige. https://mariakillam.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/2021-SW-BM-FB-Colour-Wheel-Neutral-Paint-Colours.pdf", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "buckshaw", "author_name": "GiGi Buckshaw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/buckshaw", "date": "2022-03-12", "text": "Hello Everyone, I\u2019m at my wits end. I bought my Mom\u2019s condo on Anna Maria Island Florida when she passed and decided to completely renovate it. I\u2019m a novice but got plenty of advice from my new neighbors who had already been through the process. After deciding the scope of work I interviewed a few contractors. I chose one who was actually in the high-end because he promised that I \u201cwould never have to worry about anything\u201d. He quoted $79,660.00 for labor and rough materials . He also, charged a separate fee if $1,000 for permits. In September I paid a down payment of $31,000 but the project didn\u2019t start until November (it\u2019s now March). I\u2019m living in Michigan because my condo is uninhabitable. On December 4th I get an email telling me that everything is going great inferring things are getting done. He asks for the mid job payment of $ 24,380.00 and I fed ex him a certified check  I\u2019m a flight attendant so it\u2019s easy for me to jump on a flight so I  go down and stay with my neighbor for a few days on December 28th. I understand it\u2019s a construction site but they didn\u2019t cover anything like they promised (televisions and new appliances and vanities are full of drywall dust), black mold in the kitchen because a pipe was leaking. main_question: {"author_id": "amylou321", "author_name": "amylou321", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/amylou321", "date": "2022-03-13", "text": "Has anyone here heard of or used the app Cronometer? I had heard the name in passing before and after restarting my diet after a somewhat disheartening incident I decided to try it. It was a touch confusing at first but I really like it. A doctor that I went to a few years ago whose practice exclusively saw patients who wanted to lose weight told me that the best practice is to keep a food journal or use some sort of app to track everything. I usually use my fitbit app to do it, but the trouble with that was I had no real option to log homemade recipes except to log every single ingredient separately. A YouTuber I watch mentioned that they are able to create their recipes and depending on the amount of servings you designated for that recipe, calculate the important macros in it. That is what I needed and I really like it. While I log things on the app on my phone, I use my desktop at work to log in to the website and create my recipes on it to save to my account. I even put the most simple things that I may eat everyday as a \"recipe.\" For example, I have a recipe saved for scrambled eggs with cheese, so that I do not have to go in there every day and lookup and log eggs, butter, and cheese separately. The peat moss has a pH of 3.5 on its own.   Assume the other ingredients in your soil mix have a pH of 6.5.   Is there any formula you can use - based on the percent of the two ingredients in your soil mix - to estimate the target pH of the resulting soil mix?   As a use case, assume the soil has 20% of the peat moss and 80% of the \"other\" ingredients. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "toxcrusadr", "author_name": "toxcrusadr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/toxcrusadr", "date": "2022-03-18", "text": "Not only that, but there are buffering effects. Weak acids and bases do not respond linearly to the addition of more acid or base. Most relevant to soil systems is the carbonate-bicarbonate equilibrium. Carbonate can exist in the form of insoluble carbonate salts like calcium carbonate, or dissolved carbonate and bicarbonate. And there's atmospheric CO2 as well.  The ratio between carbonate and bicarbonate in solution (in soil pore water) will depend on the pH.  But if you start adding acid or base, the pH of a carbonate system will not even change linearly. It has flat and steep places along the way. Getting back to what you said, it should be SORT OF linear though.  The mix you described might settle somewhere around 6.  Only one way to find out. I would like the first mix I make to be at least close to the target.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2022-03-18", "text": "@tapla Do you have any rules of thumb you use to predict the final pH of a soil, given the parameters in my question?", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "toxcrusadr", "author_name": "toxcrusadr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/toxcrusadr", "date": "2022-03-21", "text": "I don't.  Doesn't mean there aren't any, but I haven't tried to do this.  If you have consistent inputs - the same peat moss and the same other ingredients - you can make a mix and try it out and see. If you are creating something like the 5-1-1 mix that comes so frequently recommended for a multitude of container growing situations, peat plays a very small role....as it should :-) And the pH of peat is pretty variable, ranging from 3.0 to 4.5 so a strict formulaic application is not going to be all that helpful. The inclusion of the lime initially is to buffer the immediate acidity created by the use of the bark and the peat in the mix so that it does not shock newly potted plants that may not be accustomed to extremes. But the lime leaches out over time anyway and the media will approximate a more moderate level of acidity. The need for frequent fertilization negates any nutrient issues that might be impacted by a pH is that is slightly too high or too low. I am a big proponent of the 5-1-1, which I have used for many years as I find it ideal for just about any container planting situation. But instead of peat, I use a similar volume of a high quality potting mix (also heavy on the bark and very light on the peat) which is already pH buffered and I have never added any additional lime. I don't even own any lime :-) Granted, most of what I am growing are acid lovers or the vast majority of plants that prefer an acidic soil but I have never encountered any issues by omitting the lime altogether. btw, the recipe for the 5-1-1 suggests 1 Tbsp of dolomitic lime for every gallon of blended mix. westes, I have to admire your inquiring mind for wanting to nail down all the details involved with these soil issues.
