title: Using Garden Waste Compost as a Substitute for Bark | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2022-03-13", "text": "In a raised bed, what are the reasons that you might prefer using bark over garden waste compost?  In a container situation, I understand that carefully sized bark helps to control the hydrology of water in the container, by lowering the perched water table.   In a raised bed that concern goes away, so it might be more about the relative ability of each type of ingredient to hold nutrients.   Let's consider this question in the context of a plant that does well in bark soils, such as Azalea, Rhododendron, or Camellia.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "In a raised bed, what are the reasons that you might prefer using bark over garden waste compost? Not all OM is created equal. In large part, it depends on whether or not the compost is finished. Unfinished compost can be expected to immobilize nitrogen (N). which often leads to the grower applying toxic levels of what nutrients are in fertilizers other than N, and structural changes related to a decrease in the size of soil particles. Conifer bark is rich in lignin and suberin, naturally occurring bipolymers that contribute to resistance of the breakdown of media particles, which limits N immobilization and breakdown of the particles. Hardwood bark generally does not contain as much of these bipolymers and breaks down faster, contributing to N immobilization. Hardwood bark is also related to pH spikes that occur during the breakdown of cellulose and other compounds that readily decay.   A handful of what is in my raised beds. It started as a mixture of bark/ sand, Turface, reed/ sedge peat. The image was taken about 10 years after the beds were made. My contributions to the contents of the beds over the years has been limited to only the media removed from the roots of plants during repotting sessions, which is based almost entirely on equal measures of conifer bark/ Turface/ granite or cherrystone. The medium remains so friable that I can plunge my hand into the soil to a depth of more than 6\" with little resistance, yet it retains plenty of air, and moisture except during prolonged spells of hot/ dry/ windy summer weather when I might need to water every 4-5 days. A general rule is a raised bed needn't contain any more than 10-15% OM, and OM that breaks down slowly should be preferred. I would guess that the OM content of the soil currently in my RBs is in excess of 50%, and I'm extremely happy with how productive it is and has been. title: Trying to avoid builder overages | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mauro-zammarano", "author_name": "Mauro Zammarano", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mauro-zammarano", "date": "2022-03-13", "text": "Hello, first of all, I apologize for my lengthy question, but here it goes.... I have a design contract with a builder and I am slowly finalizing the home design. I did not sign a contract with this builder yet, except the design contract. The builder uses allowances for: Appliances, Cabinets, Countertops, Tile and Flooring, Home Automation and Security, Hardware, Plumbing Fixtures, Decorative Electrical Fixtures, Front Door. For each overage there is a hefty 25% extra charge from the builder. If I spend less than the allowance for a category  I get the left over allowance +25% back. So obviously I would like to minimize my expenses in these categories but still do just enough to get a certificate of occupancy and then install, upgrade later without a 25% overcharge. Does this sounds like a good idea to you? For example for cabinets the allowance is about $30-35 and with that we would likely be able to do cabinets for kitchen but not bathrooms. Or I could just plug a cheap fridge and electric range with hood for the inspection and then build the actual kitchen cabinetry and proper appliances later on.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "res2architect", "author_name": "res2architect", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/res2architect", "date": "2022-03-13", "text": "I've never known a builder to supply kitchen appliances. You're thinking of the 25% contractor markup as an extra but if the allowance amount had been accurately estimated, that cost would already be in the allowance. The real problem is 25% is very high and might be inflated above the builder's normal OH&P % but it might also be due to the local market .... something to deal with up front when first interviewing contractors. Another problem is who the builder buys from; you'll never know the subcontractor or supplier's markup and often there is no competitive pricing. This process is unique to homebuilding; a commercial project would require competitive sub contractor/supplier bids for allowances similar to a Cost P;us contract. At any rate, pick out as much as possible now or supply it yourself and avoid allowances. Also, you should be carrying a healthy contingnecy in your budget.  Its not possible to predict the final cost of a building.", "images": []}}

title: Neptune, 1909 or Harvey Jones kitchens | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kate-thomson66", "author_name": "Kate Thomson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kate-thomson66", "date": "2022-03-13", "text": "Hi, we'd really like an in frame solid timber kitchen and like the shaker style but with beading details. Kitchens we've seen so far that we like are Neptune's Chichester range, the 1909 Georgian range and the Harvey Jones original range. Does anyone have any experience of these kitchens and any recommendations for which is better or any to avoid please? If you know of any similar kitchens we'd love to hear about them too. We're in Yorkshire so need a stockist in this area. Many Thanks.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1385883894", "author_name": "Lifestyle Kitchens", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1385883894", "date": "2022-04-06", "text": "@margretg2 This is true that the majority of shaker kitchen doors have a solid timber frame, if its painted than its usually an ash frame, but the centre panel is an oak or ash veneer. This is because the panel is thinner and if it was a solid timber it could be prone to movement so being a veneered mdf or chipboard means a more stable door. Neptune use a hardwood ply for their centre panels (according to their brochure-also in their brochure they say that they've moved some of their production to a purpose built facility in China) Other factors to look for in a quality shaker frame is along the tenon joints, a cheaper door has a V groove along the joint as this masks any assembly defects and any hairline cracks due to movement that may appear over time. A smooth tenon joint is completely flat/smooth and can be reinforced with dowels to help prevent any later movement. Also consider with timber is how the log is cut. There's 3 main ways timber is cut for furniture. The cheapest timber cut is plainsawn and has the cathedral arch characteristics and is just slices along the length of the log, this is more prone to movement/splitting (but is used with walnut to display the natural woodgrain). Quarter sawn (traditional and modern cut) is a more expensive way to cut logs but is ideal for oak giving a straight grain and is used for quality furniture especially if its to be lacquered. Finally there's rift sawn which is the most expensive cut and characterized for its clean sleek lines.", "images": []}}

title: Centerpiece tree for new garden, maybe a Blue Chinese Wisteria? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jason-carlton26", "author_name": "Jason, zone 7A, near Greensboro NC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jason-carlton26", "date": "2022-03-13", "text": "I have a new garden space, it was going to be a fruit and nut orchard but now I'm thinking to just make it ornamental. About the Garden Area The new garden is roughly 100' long and 75' wide. It's not enclosed, so I have to worry about local wildlife; mainly deer, rabbits, racoons, opossum, squirrels, birds, voles, moles, snakes, and coyotes. And the occasional fox or wild turkey. I want to attract many of them (not moles, voles, and coyotes, of course), so I need plants that are tough enough to not be damaged by the occasional nibble or trample. Or taste bad so that the animals aren't going to eat them. The ground is on a slight slope, direct sun from around 9am with evening shade from wild trees on the Western side. I've recently taken down field pine, red oak, hickory, poplar, and maple trees, along with a ton of greenbrier. The tree stumps will probably just be cut below ground level and covered up. I'll be running sprinklers, so there shouldn't be an issue of watering. Nearby is a mature Tulip Poplar that blooms red late-February through early-April, then it's green for the rest of the year. There's also a White Dogwood that blooms white from around April through May. Both are similarly sized at about 30' high. The backdrop is American holly, followed by wild woods. Surrounding flowers and plants All of these are just plants that I already have that could easily be extended to this area. Flowers that I have on hand are purple irises, yellow irises, yellow and white daffodils, white lilies, yellow canna lilies, Asiatic lilies, Devil's Trumpet (Datura, large purplish-black flowers), Moonflower (also Datura, with large white flowers that open in the evenings), Autumn Joy sedum, speedwell, salvia, purple phlox, and I have no idea how many annuals seeds. I'll probably plant orange / red habanero nearby. And I can take cuttings of butterfly bushes (purple), Sunshine Ligustrum (yellow), and Ever Red Fringe Flower (red). For ground cover I have mondo grass, Chocolate Chip Ajuga, Creeping Jenny, and Anne Marie ivy. I also have a Blue Java banana tree that needs to go somewhere, but it will probably be closer to the end of this garden. And I can surround it with canna lilies and maybe elephant ears, since the leaves are similar. In addition, I had set aside $1000 for this new garden so I can buy other plants. Future Plan In my dream world, I'll be adding a water bog and 2 koi / goldfish cascading ponds near this garden area. I have a 1000G pond in my back yard that I love, and I really want to extend the look to the front of the house. I'm really not a fan of lawns, anyway, so my long term goal is to convert almost an acre of lawn in to usable and pretty flower gardens, with maybe 1/4 acre left for grass. Now for the Question I am considering a centerpiece tree that would be surrounded by bushes, flowers, and ornamental grasses. I would love to find something that does well in my area (zone 7a) but isn't overly common. It needs to be smaller than the tulip tree and dogwood, a different color than those two trees, and it would be great if I had a longer season of color. Crape myrtles would work, but are pretty common. Then I came across this: https://www.naturehills.com/blue-chinese-wisteria?id=8018 The pictures are beautiful, it seems to be tough and hardy, and I don't know that I've ever seen one. What's the catch? Is this an actual tree, or a vine that's just shaped to look like a tree? I found this article that scared me: https://www.thespruce.com/chinese-wisteria-plants-2132898", "images": []}

title: (OT) What's going on at the farm | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2022-03-14", "text": "The drought continues, with no precipitation since the snow of February 15, and no rain in the two week forecast.  I estimate our total precipitation for 2022 so far at about 1 1/2\".  This is shaping up to be another 2017, an awful year, when the province ran completely out of water and it had to be brought in by truck over the Apennines from Genova, while we roasted in 100\u00b0-plus temperatures.  Our neighbors' pond didn't go dry, and they allowed us to water our new and potted plants from that once the watering ban kicked in in June.  If it happens again, at least we'll know what to expect. I'm very much on edge on account of the war in Ukraine.  The European Union has made an agreement for all member states to share care of the Ukrainian refugees, and I think we'll see a capillary spread of these unfortunates over the continent.  The last I heard Italy had received about 35,000, with more to come.  We've put in a request to host a family, but so far have heard nothing back from the mayor's office.  Gas prices, always high by U.S. standards, have gone through the roof:  the current price is about $9-$10 a gallon.  God knows what will happen there and with food prices and supplies.  I'm glad I'm vegetarian, my groceries should be less affected by grain shortages (I think). I'm NEVER caught up on the garden work (or housework either, but that doesn't matter).  The last few days I've been working around the Rock.  This is a fair-sized outcropping in one of the fields.  I may have written about it before and be now repeating myself, but, time for an update.  The Rock is crumbling sedimentary stone phasing to soil, and home to a population of trees, some of them otherwise rare on our property.  The most common are flowering ash, laburnums, and redtwig dogwood, with, in addition, wild plum (blackthorn), and a few oaks, wild pears, wild cherries, checker trees (Sorbus torminalis), hawthorn, and Viburnum lantana.  The most striking trees are probably the laburnums:  these are the largest specimens I've ever seen, multi-trunked and tree-sized; and I'm glad to have the couple of checker trees, as I know of only one other place on our property they grow, and they're a desirable species and not overly common.  I'd like to have Cornelian cherry (Cornus mas), which grows close by, as well, and may plant one or two this fall in the shade of the north side.  I would also like hophornbeam, which grows close by, but can't figure out a place to put it.  Years ago in a burst of optimism and ignorance DH and I planted seedling flowering ash all around the base of the Rock; amazingly, most of them survived, and some have grown into young trees.  That's a tough plant.  There were two cultivated cherries planted at the north side of the Rock, but one has died, from age I think, and the other is senescent. Two years ago, during the Covid quarantine, I did a thorough cleanup of the Rock, cutting down and chopping up brambles and wild clematis, pruning and cutting out dead wood on the trees, and selectively cutting and thinning wild plum and redtwig dogwood.  I'm not a fan of either of these last two species, but the dogwood grows where nothing else does, and the ground needs something to do; and the thorny tangled wild plum guards the desirable trees, making it harder for the deer to get in and rub the bark off their trunks and break their branches.  It's pretty in flower, too. The cleanup is going faster this year than two years ago, the brush not having had time to recover fully.  The wild plum is the worst:  it suckers madly and extends its wicked branches out in all directions, and I want to leave enough to form a guard, but not more.  Brambles I slaughter without compunction, and wild clematis, though it's not doing much.  Things look much as they did two years ago, a little less messy, and with the old pruned matter decaying into the soil.  I think the Rock will be a pleasant sight once I've finished.  I ponder additions, such as Cornelian cherry, and woodland floor flowers, in which the adjacent woodland of the neighbors is rich.  They're in bloom now, erythroniums, primroses, and hepaticas, and are a lovely sight.  Primroses might work, as they appear to love dank shady conditions, but I think the others might demand better soil.  Well, perhaps erythroniums.  We do have violets which grow everywhere.  All in all I'm happy with what I see, and looking forward to better in coming years..", "images": []}

title: (OT) What's going on at the farm | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2022-03-14", "text": "Note:  I wrote this this morning and posted it, but it never showed up on the forum.  Seasiderooftop's experience strengthened my suspicious that mention of a certain European country caused my post not to show up.  So I invented a substitute for the country's name, which you will see below, and my revised post appeared.  (I'll see if it survives this edit.) I don't appreciate this action of Houzz. The drought continues, with no precipitation since the snow of February 15, and no rain in the two week forecast. I estimate our total precipitation for 2022 so far at about 1 1/2\". This is shaping up to be another 2017, an awful year, when the province ran completely out of water and it had to be brought in by truck over the Apennines from Genova, while we roasted in 100\u00b0-plus temperatures. Our neighbors' pond didn't go dry, and they allowed us to water our new and potted plants from that once the watering ban kicked in in June. If it happens again, at least we'll know what to expect. I'm very much on edge on account of the war in the yellow-blue country. The European Union has made an agreement for all member states to share care of the yellow-blue country refugees, and I think we'll see a capillary spread of these unfortunates over the continent. The last I heard Italy had received about 35,000, with more to come. We've put in a request to host a family, but so far have heard nothing back from the mayor's office. Gas prices, always high by U.S. standards, have gone through the roof: the current price is about $9-$10 a gallon. God knows what will happen there and with food prices and supplies. I'm glad I'm vegetarian, my groceries should be less affected by grain shortages (I think). I'm NEVER caught up on the garden work (or housework either, but that doesn't matter). The last few days I've been working around the Rock. This is a fair-sized outcropping in one of the fields. I may have written about it before and be now repeating myself, but, time for an update. The Rock is crumbling sedimentary stone phasing to soil, and home to a population of trees, some of them otherwise rare on our property. The most common are flowering ash, laburnums, and redtwig dogwood, with, in addition, wild plum (blackthorn), and a few oaks, wild pears, wild cherries, checker trees (Sorbus torminalis), hawthorn, and Viburnum lantana. The most striking trees are probably the laburnums: these are the largest specimens I've ever seen, multi-trunked and tree-sized; and I'm glad to have the couple of checker trees, as I know of only one other place on our property they grow, and they're a desirable species and not overly common. I'd like to have Cornelian cherry (Cornus mas), which grows close by, as well, and may plant one or two this fall in the shade of the north side. I would also like hophornbeam, which grows close by, but can't figure out a place to put it. Years ago in a burst of optimism and ignorance DH and I planted seedling flowering ash all around the base of the Rock; amazingly, most of them survived, and some have grown into young trees. That's a tough plant. There were two cultivated cherries planted at the north side of the Rock, but one has died, from age I think, and the other is senescent. Two years ago, during the Covid quarantine, I did a thorough cleanup of the Rock, cutting down and chopping up brambles and wild clematis, pruning and cutting out dead wood on the trees, and selectively cutting and thinning wild plum and redtwig dogwood. I'm not a fan of either of these last two species, but the dogwood grows where nothing else does, and the ground needs something to do; and the thorny tangled wild plum guards the desirable trees, making it harder for the deer to get in and rub the bark off their trunks and break their branches. It's pretty in flower, too. The cleanup is going faster this year than two years ago, the brush not having had time to recover fully. The wild plum is the worst: it suckers madly and extends its wicked branches out in all directions, and I want to leave enough to form a guard, but not more. Brambles I slaughter without compunction, and wild clematis, though it's not doing much. Things look much as they did two years ago, a little less messy, and with the old pruned matter decaying into the soil. I think the Rock will be a pleasant sight once I've finished. I ponder additions, such as Cornelian cherry, and woodland floor flowers, in which the adjacent woodland of the neighbors is rich. They're in bloom now, erythroniums, primroses, and hepaticas, and are a lovely sight. Primroses might work, as they appear to love dank shady conditions, but I think the others might demand better soil. Well, perhaps erythroniums. We do have violets which grow everywhere. All in all I'm happy with what I see, and looking forward to better in coming years.", "images": []}

title: Orientación ideal para porcelánico rectangular en porche. O cuadrado? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "thdros74", "author_name": "DA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/thdros74", "date": "2022-03-14", "text": "Buenas tardes. Estamos eligiendo suelo porcel\u00e1nico de exterior en formato grande para el porche exterior. Es estilo piedra con veta, moderno. El porche orientado al sur-sureste, a continuaci\u00f3n del porche el jard\u00edn. En el interior de la vivienda tenemos suelo porcel\u00e1nico imitaci\u00f3n madera  (22x120 cm) orientado en el sentido de la carpinter\u00eda exterior. La salida exterior al jard\u00edn a trav\u00e9s de grandes puertas oscilo paralelas, lo que da una continuidad hacia el exterior. La pregunta es si para el porche un formato 60x120 cm habr\u00eda que colocarlo tambi\u00e9n de forma paralela a la carpinter\u00eda exterior (el lado de 120 cm), es decir lado largo paralelo al porcel\u00e1nico de interior,  o si tambi\u00e9n es posible colocarlo de forma perpendicular a la carpinter\u00eda (lado de 60 cm). La duda es porque colocado de forma paralela tenemos m\u00e1s desperdicio de material y no se ajusta tan bien a la forma del porche. En cambio en sentido perpendicular s\u00ed se ajusta bien, pero tenemos dudas de que sea lo m\u00e1s apropiado. Otra opci\u00f3n es optar por un formato 75x75cm, que tambi\u00e9n se ajusta muy bien a la forma del porche. Gracias por vuestra colaboraci\u00f3n", "images": []}

We hired a designer to help use draft/design a renovation to an old home we own. After about 6 months, and around $25,000 we submitted for development permit and to general contractors for quotes. Our budget to start was around $450,000 - and we agreed we indicated we could push it to about $600,000 in order to do an addition and a garage. All three contractors provided quotes over over $1m - ranging from $1m to $1.4. The city indicated that the additions we wanted were not going to be approved due to lot coverage issues. At this point we had has a long process and with this person and we just wanted to move on and have someone else complete the design. We asked her to send us all work we had paid for to date. She send a CAD file that was stripped of all layers, line weights etc. Essentially a line drawing with exterior measurements. She send the .pdfs for various facades, elevations etc. as well. She indicates she will not release the layered CAD to us. My questions is how she thinks this is appropriate? If we were to continue with her she would presumably have to release the CAD to the builder at some point. Further, the drawings can not be used on ay other property given they are specific to this renovation and not a new build/in-fill. This has occurred in Calgary, Alberta. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jreynolds-01", "author_name": "jreynolds_01", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jreynolds-01", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "Im no pro but I do enjoy DIY of my lawn. If you havent already,,,you need to do a soil test.  You can start with your agriculture agency;or,  find a commercial one. Go from there. If you dont do that.  At least determine your grass type so you know the proper amount of fert to put on your yard. Good luck, John", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2022-03-18", "text": "You've heard the term, winterize, but maybe are not aware how it works.  You apply a strong nitrogen fertilizer after the grass has fully stopped growing.  Usually this is in late November.  You wait until the grass has turned off, but the roots are not frozen.  Then when you  apply the nitrogen, the roots can take it up and store if for the winter.  In the spring the roots will be fully charged as the temps rise.  Fully charged means that you do NOT need to add more fertilizer at this time.  Even with no winterizing, the roots work with the soil microbes to recharge.  The difference would be that with no winterizing it might take a week or so longer for the grass to awaken.  In either case the grass roots have enough stored nutrients to power through the entire spring.  That means you do not need to fertilize early.  Yes, I realize this advice flies in the face of all the people trying to sell you more fertilizer (than you need), but it works just fine if you don't do anything until May (warmer grasses) or late May (cooler grasses).  The stores are packed with fertilizers and the airwaves are filled with people selling fertilizer, but NOW IS NOT THE TIME to apply.  Save it for Memorial Day.  Even if you do apply now, you will need it again in late May for the summer heat.  Don't waste the time or money now. The 4 or 5-step programs are a way to sell products so the company owners can make their boat payments all year long.  You are correct to challenge the need for them.  But having said that I can outline some steps that the lawn forum communities have come up with over the past couple of decades.  You can call them steps or not - potato/potahto. That is 5 steps if you want to think of it that way; however, you have many options of what you are applying and what not.  What you are not applying is any insecticide.  Not only to most lawns not need it, most soils will suffer terribly from unneeded applications of insecticide.  Microscopic insects comprise a large fraction of the soil microbes which keep your soil healthy.  If you apply insecticide, as is included in the Scott's summer application, you are going to change the balance of fungi, bacteria, and microarthropods (teensy insects) in the soil.  The soil microbe populations will eventually rebalance, but why do the damage in the first place??  Most lawns don't have a problem.  In my own (anecdotal) experience of 55 years of lawn keeping, I have never needed an insecticidd.  And I might say that the advertising you see in the summer will lead you to believe your lawn is suffering from grubs, army worms, spiders, ants, or some other bug, but it almost never is.  If you believe you have an insect problem, please write to a forum to ask.  There are simple tests you can do to verify a problem and then make an informed decision about which products to use and how to use them.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "Hard to establish, very susceptible to root rot if not in excellent soil conditions and IME, marginal in a zone 7 unless in a very sheltered position.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "ken-adrian", "author_name": "ken_adrian Adrian MI cold Z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ken-adrian", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "it appears its zone appropriate ... and if so .. then its demise may be related to planting.. watering or extraordinary winter ... if you want to try to figure it out.. you will need to provide us with significant info on all those things ... may as well throw in you big city location as well ... ken https://duckduckgo.com/?q=Edgeworthia+%27akebono%27+zone&t=ffcm&ia=web", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "How \"zone appropriate\" this plant is is up for discussion. If you have not grown it, then just relying on Internet (mis)information is not likely to give you valid or sound data. An established plant may well be able to tolerate a \"typical\" zone 7 winter. But that tolerance drops significantly for any newly planted Edgeworthia, as they are notoriously slow and somewhat difficult to establish. Since the flower buds develop in summer for the following season, they are subject to cold damage, specially late season cold damage, that will prevent any flowering. And even result in significant stem dieback. I would never attempt to grow Edgeworthia in a zone 7 garden unless in a very sheltered/protected location with some reflected heat. Akebono is also reportedly less tolerant of cold. While there is some ongoing discussion as to the distinction between the two common species under cultivation, Akebono is a cultivar of E. papyrifera, a less robust, less hardy and non-fragrant form of paperbush. The intensely colored forms all tend to be of this species, rather than E chyrsantha, which only offers cream to yellow flowers, but highly fragrant.", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "alan-mciver", "author_name": "Alan McIver", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/alan-mciver", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "Have had E. chrysantha here for 20 years, really thriving.  So I assume Akebono is not as tolerant but will, nevertheless, try one more time, if I find one I can carry home at a reasonable price. title: Has the loss of a single business or building in your area... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2022-03-15", "text": "This may be hard to answer or almost irrelevant to those in car-centric or spread out/ rural areas, but has the loss of a single business or building in your area had a major impact on your community? I am not talking about job loss but more on a sociological level. Before I lived here, back in the 80s, my neighborhood was an area that had stalled on a number of levels. On the one hand, since the 60s sometime, it was not a bad neighborhood to live in, but up until the very early 90s, 92-93, there were lots of abandoned buildings and not a lot of solid infrastructure, if that makes sense. If you needed a hospital, you were in excellent position. If you needed a full service grocery store or wanted something that was close to fine dining, forget it. When I moved back to this city after a couple years in surburban Chicago the moves actually asked why I moved from such a nice neighborhood into a slum. It wasn't, but it was not far from that by car, and really even one block over there were two wino bars that would literally have people lying on the sidewalk out front, and a burnt out hotel (flophouse). This actually changed quite a lot the first year I was here. Anyway, sometime in the 1980s a gym opened in my neighborhood and it was in a huge building, so a number of ancillary and other social service kinds of businesses also opened in the buildings, and by 1993 or so the neighboring building opened what would be a thriving coffee shop, and a books/magazines/gifts shop, and across the street a restaurant went in the first floor of an apartment building. You would meet anybody in the neighborhood in any one of those places. As the neighborhood evolved there was also a bunch of programming for kids in that building. Fast forward to the late 20-teens and for various reasons the gym closed. (it was on seven interlocking levels, not at all universal access, things like that. Then the building sold. Because of the real estate it was bought by a developer and the building has been torn down. So that particular sort of \"real gym\" is gone, people scattered to various branches of national gyms that have sprung up, there's no book/magazine/gift store (that had disappeared earlier). And while there are Starbucks and that sort of thing, now those are not particularly social places where you meet people you didn't go there with. It's people either with someone they walked in with or people on their tablets or phones. Although the neighborhood is actually getting more and more residential, there is actually no real neighborhood anymore. Part of this is cultural change, but I think the loss of that physical building really killed the neighborhood as it was. In addition there was a long-time diner that was also sold so the site could be redeveloped. There were people that ate there every single day. Covid wiped out the diner that a lot of them migrated to, (not lack of business, lack of workers, they own two diners and only have enough reliable workers to keep one running). We also lost every fast food outlet in the vicinity. Not that I ate at McDonalds or Wendys more than about once a year, but I don't know that it's great that cheap food has been wiped off the map for people who live here.", "images": []}

title: Combination PVC and cast iron for waste lines | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-454990918", "author_name": "Paul Matuszewski", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-454990918", "date": "2022-03-16", "text": "Hey Guys, I was very concerned regarding noise in my walls/house from drainage lines. As such, in the process of planning It was recommended to use cast iron for 2nd floor to first floor/basement drops (or stacks, I'm told). This is what my contractor put in at my request. However, while going over the images of progress, I noticed that the vertical lines were indeed cast iron, but the other parts were PVC. Looking at the final product, I was a little concerned regarding the noise from the turns in the pipe. This got me to trying to figure out.. if you do a combination system.. where should the transition be? or should you just do all cast iron. It seems like any vertical section or turn into it, should be cast iron? If I have PVC in the ceiling.. am I going to hear that, despite my cast iron drop? It seems like the best way (without doing insulation) would have been to do cast iron throughout. Had   I known, I would have done the whole thing in cast iron. But I didn't.  Now, I'm left with the work already being done, so I'm sure if I change, there will be some eye rolling and increased cost. perhaps a middle ground would be to make the turn cast iron as it transitions into the vertical drop? What about down by the floor, shouldn't it be cast iron too as it turns back into the house for the final drainage?? What do you all think? Or am I over thinking this...", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/02a22d2002312bb5_9622-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "What was done is a good compromise. And yes, you are over-thinking a bit. Where you will have noise is where water has turbulence , changes directions, etc. Iron is really hard to work with - esp in that tight space between joists. You might be able to do a little bit more in the run that is parallel with the joists... but you probably won't. Cast iron is the best solution, but ask about any other solutions for the PVC (Spray foam?).", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-867564120", "author_name": "HU-867564120", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-867564120", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "As Jake points out, the noise is greatest where there is turbulence.  From experience, that is at the PVC elbows at the bottom of a vertical drop. We were finishing our basement and was concerned with the kitchen drains above. I bought this product https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07ZKLKHN5/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o09_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 and wrapped all the PVC drain lines 100%, then ran water down the drains. The elbows at the vertical drops were noisy and I ended up wrapping 3 layers over them. The pipes are now near-silent before the drywall goes up.", "images": []}}

title: Como soldar con electrodo | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "carla-jurado95", "author_name": "Lorena J", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/carla-jurado95", "date": "2022-03-16", "text": "En muchas ocasiones, las piezas met\u00e1licas a consecuencia del paso del tiempo o las condiciones climatol\u00f3gicas suelen deteriorarse hasta llegar a romperse. En muchas ocasiones se pueden substituir pero en muchas otras es imposible encontrar repuesto. Por lo que la \u00fanica soluci\u00f3n posible es la soldadura. La soldadura el\u00e9ctrica por arco con electrodo es un m\u00e9todo de soldadura homog\u00e9neo que tiene diversas aplicaciones en el sector industrial.  Al soldar con electrodo revestido, la fusi\u00f3n del metal es provocada por el intenso calor generado por un arco el\u00e9ctrico establecido al poner en contacto dos conductores de distinta polaridad: el propio electrodo y la masa el\u00e9ctrica. La protecci\u00f3n del ba\u00f1o de fusi\u00f3n se obtiene gracias a los vapores met\u00e1licos que se desprenden tras producirse la fusi\u00f3n del recubrimiento de dicho electrodo.   C\u00f3mo soldar con electrodo Antes de empezar a soldar con electrodo es imprescindible llevar a cabo las tareas de preparaci\u00f3n de fondos y del soporte necesarias para facilitar y garantizar un acabado de calidad. Estas son las operaciones requeridas: -Efectuar una preparaci\u00f3n de las juntas de uni\u00f3n acorde al espesor del metal. -Eliminar pinturas, revestimientos y \u00f3xidos sobre la junta de uni\u00f3n y su periferia. -Desengrasar la zona de soldadura -Presentar, alinear, sujetar y revisar la posici\u00f3n de los metales a unir antes de efectuar la soldadura. Una vez realizada la preparaci\u00f3n del soporte, se procede a la elecci\u00f3n del electrodo m\u00e1s acorde al tipo de trabajo a realizar, teniendo en cuenta los siguientes aspectos: -La naturaleza del material a soldar, para que el electrodo disponga de un alma igual o compatible. -El espesor de los metales a unir. A modo de referencia, para espesores de 1,5 o 2 mm se emplean di\u00e1metros de electrodo de 1,6 o 2 mm; para espesores de entre 2 y 3 mm, electrodos de 2 o 2,5 mm; para espesores de entre 2 y 5 mm, electrodos de entre 2,5 y 3,2 mm; y para espesores superiores a los 5 mm, electrodos a partir de los 3,2 mm. El proceso para soldar con electrodo empieza con la regulaci\u00f3n del equipo. Hay que relacionar los di\u00e1metros de electrodo con las corrientes de soldadura recomendadas.  Con la m\u00e1quina ajustada, se escogen metales de iguales caracter\u00edsticas a las de aquellos que se van a soldar y se efect\u00faan distintas pruebas de soldadura para afinar la regulaci\u00f3n del equipo y determinar la t\u00e9cnica de ejecuci\u00f3n m\u00e1s adecuada.   Una vez el equipo est\u00e1 perfectamente regulado y est\u00e1 clara la t\u00e9cnica que se debe utilizar, se inicia el proceso de soldadura de los metales de la siguiente forma: En primer lugar, es necesario cebar el electrodo y el arco el\u00e9ctrico. Para ello, se arrastra varias veces el electrodo por una superficie met\u00e1lica de desecho con el objetivo de calentar la punta y evitar que se pegue al metal. Se prosigue con la colocaci\u00f3n del electrodo en su posici\u00f3n correcta respecto a los metales. Cuando se suelde en posici\u00f3n plana horizontal o vertical, el \u00e1ngulo que debe formar el electrodo respecto a las piezas es de 90\u00b0, mientras que cuando la uni\u00f3n forme \u00e1ngulo debe ser de 45\u00b0. Una vez posicionado el electrodo, hay que transferir al mismo el \u00e1ngulo de desplazamiento sin perder el de colocaci\u00f3n. Para posici\u00f3n plana horizontal, el \u00e1ngulo de desplazamiento es de unos 60\u00b0 respecto a la horizontal; para posici\u00f3n vertical, de unos 10\u00b0 respecto a la vertical; y para uniones en \u00e1ngulo, unos 30\u00b0 respecto a la vertical. Con el electrodo bien posicionado y con su \u00e1ngulo de desplazamiento adecuado, se acerca el electrodo a la pieza para que salte el arco el\u00e9ctrico y se inicie la fusi\u00f3n del metal y del alma. Desde que se inicia el proceso de fusi\u00f3n del metal y hasta que finaliza la soldadura, se deben seguir las siguientes premisas para obtener un cord\u00f3n de est\u00e9tica y dimensiones adecuadas: Asegurarse de que se mantiene la distancia desoldadura correcta durante el avance de esta y a medida que se consume el electrodo. title: Buttermilk Beignet Hamentaschen | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "plllog", "author_name": "plllog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/plllog", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "It's Purim.  The feast of Esther.  A fun festival when we give baskets of food to everybody.  Hamentaschen are a favorite.  Triangular pastries representing the garb of the villain of the story which get gobbled down as we make noise to drown out his name.  I received a Purim basket with a few crumbly cookie hamentaschen, which are good, but are very different the yeast dough ones everybody made when I was growing up.  Today was (was going to be) a wild day and I knew I wasn't going to have time, but last night I was thinking about our late, beloved 2ManyDirversions, who was planning with me to make beignets to the point where she suggested that we end each forum post with the word \"beignets\".  It was fun and silly and weird, and the memory brought the idea that it would only take a couple of hours to make them. I found the buttermilk beignet recipe on Epicurious, while just looking for fluffy enough to stuff. (https://www.epicurious.com/recipes/food/views/buttermilk-beignets-356850, but a limited access site.) I woke up in time.  I was still tired, so put in 1.5 x the amount of baking soda, but the buttermilk was particularly acidy so I figured it would just make them fluffier.  (They were really fluffy!)  Instead of trying to stuff them with a pastry bag, I cut a little hole in the top, and spooned in the blueberry compote I made. (Thawed blueberries in their own juice (frozen from fresh), zest of a blood orange, big spoon of sugar, little slug of Cointreau.) The recipe called for twice the powdered sugar that you think you need, but I used my sugar shaker and needed lots less than I'd thought.  And, of course, I cut them into triangles.  Since I was in a rush, I didn't bother with uniformity, and fried up the little ones from the ends as well as the \"real\" ones.  I divided the dough into four manageable pieces.  This also meant that if I ran into the time for my morning meeting, I could just put the rest in the fridge, but I did finish on time.  To cut them, I made an oblong of dough, rested my rolling pin at the edge and used my resin marshmallow cutter (looks like a big pizza wheel with holes in it) along the rolling pin as a straight edge, and again on a 60\u00b0 angle (by eyeball), then cut the diamonds across the middle, from obtuse angle to obtuse angle. The recipe said that it took 20 minutes to heat the oil.  I used safflower rather than the suggested peanut oil, but I think it's maybe induction rather than gas that didn't take nearly that (phew!).  I wasn't that diligent on uniformity again, but they all came up a nice, dark brown, with a little snap but well short of a crunch.  The insides are fluffy and soft with big bubbles, but a consistent texture--no breakage of the bubble walls.  Very tasty but could have used a pinch more salt and sugar, or maybe some malt.  The recipe said \"bread flour\", but I didn't want to go heavy, so I used Gold Medal Better for Bread. They were a hit!  The compote isn't very portable, so made a kit with a paper coffee cup of the compote to apply later.  I had unstuffed \"testers\" for breakfast. :) Happy Purim!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c382c8d80232c7ed_5151-w500-h403-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Planning permission | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "sana-ghauri", "author_name": "Sana Ghauri", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sana-ghauri", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "Hello,We are about to start a full house renovation and will be adding a double storey side and single storey rear extension.I wanted to ask about planning permission. How much of the design of the build needs to be decided for the planning stage? Of course I understand the main structure etc. needs to be decided but how about things like the size of the windows (not location as I know that needs to be determined beforehand) / bi-folds or sliding doors/ external appearance of the extension (i.e. left as brick or rendered). Does this all need to be specified for planning permission?Any advice would be greatly appreciated!Thanks!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-41167996975", "author_name": "Ricky Watkins", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-41167996975", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "Yes you will need detailed building regs drawings from your architect, so that the local building regs inspector can read & refer too on site visits.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "fch42", "author_name": "Frank", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fch42", "date": "2022-03-18", "text": "Planning Policies rather frequently concern themselves with \"the look of the streetscape\" and focus rather strongly on the \"Outside\" - what materials extensions are built in, window types / sizes / placement, style and shape of roofs and so on. Speaking pointedly, out of sight out of mind, what one can't see from the street concerns the planners little. In any case, most planning departments offer a \"free consultation\", a chat with a planning officer on the phone for half an hour about planning / the plans you're hoping to submit. Check with your local planning department whether they offer this service. You can ask them open questions, \"what level of detail do we need to provide in the application for materials, finishes, windows, doors, sizing, ...\", \"what do our local planning policies suggest we should do for external finishes\", \"how can we obscure views from large upper-storey windows so that we're not overlooked / we're not overlooking\", or \"what kind of changes, should site conditions require it, can we make after without invalidating the planning permit once given\". It's usually better to ask thus openly than to \"request\" (I.e. don't tell them \"on our listed building we intend to use bright flourescent pink window frames on a huge 3m x 4m glazed wall for the front dormer with protruding balcony that you're hopefully going to approve ... is that ok ?\", if you know what I mean).", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "haru-design-pfvwgb-pf~2084092253", "author_name": "Haru Design", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/haru-design-pfvwgb-pf~2084092253", "date": "2022-03-18", "text": "Frank, you've absolutely smashed this answer! title: 2019 and newer Bosch dishwashers in general | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-904733186", "author_name": "J C", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-904733186", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "Because there are many many many old threads and videos on Bosch dishwashers, the facts about them are limited when purchasing a new Bosch Dishwasher.I recently purchased a 300 series for its design with front panel buttons, and did not feel a 800 series was worth what I needed. The 500 series did not offer the same panel layout, so I searched high and low to verify what is good, better and weak between the dishwashers.So here it is... if you are planing on an upgrade or new first time purchaser of a Bosch dishwasher.500 series and below offer pretty much the same cleaning, but there are small upgrades shared between them. As of recent all carry upgraded door springs. If you are familiar with door spring issues of the past, Bosch redesigned the door springs to be robust for long term operation. Though on the 100 and 300 series lines, the door springs seem to be a wee over powering. Meaning the door will want to slam shut when half way opened. I prefer a softer action, so I ordered the new style spring kit for the 500 series, that uses a wee lighter spring tension, for the auto pop open air drying feature. The door now closes nicely with user control. Now I can pop open the door manually to give an extra dry at the last 20 minutes of the cycle, and it will stay cracked open.As for plastics not drying. I found on the 300 and 800 series with 3rd rack to hold water more than the myway rack on higher end 800 series. To combat water retention, I spray H1 food industry comptible dry lubricant coating on all sides of the plastics that are all the baskets, racks, and 3rd rack. The dry lubrucant sheds water and makes the roller wheel action a wee smoother.You may need to reapply the H1 dry lubrucant coating once a month depending on how much you use the disinfect mode and harshness of detergent.I chose to replace the 3rd rack with a flexible 3d rack, as the myway rack was not adjustable, in limiting how the upper rack was used. Other than that the myway rack would shed more water for better drying.As for upper and lower racks, you can replace the upper rack wheel assembly with the roller bearing type used in top end 500 and 800 series, if you like. But the dry lubricant works fine to assist with less friction when racks are loaded.The biggest and best upgrade was the flexible flatware baskets, as they lock together side by side or back to back. The originals used in 100, 300 and 500 series were light weight and the long single basket was limiting flexiblity. The dual half length baskets were light weight as well, and the top lids easy to break. The flexible basket set will not break and fits nicer in the lower rack. Being heaver plastic, its mass helps keep it sturdy in place when bumped or filled with tall and top heavy utensils.In a nut shell a basic 300 series can be nicely upgraded within a budget to a deluxe varient without hassles. As most all interior components can be swapped out between the lines, though the 100 series would need 3rd rack rails to be installed if adding the non existant 3rd rack, of choice.If you find you need more flexibility in the upper or lower rack, any 800 series rack will fit and function, while allowing for the fullest flexibility available with Bosch design.As for all the past complaints about Bosch dishwashers, most all are resolved at various degrees with the newer designs, even though they may look like designs of the past.", "images": []}

title: How often are dwarf conifers grafted | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "a1an", "author_name": "a1an", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/a1an", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "Just got into dwarfs conifer plantings, etc. In my youtube feeds, a few popped up showing the growers just taking cutting and then grafting a sliver on. What is the role of the grafting of the understock vs  own root. The ones I have ordered don't have any listings whether there are own root vs . graft. Anyone care to share on some newbie 101 - are most confiers grafted on a different understock, etc ? I did order 1 in standard form and that was clearly listed as Firma understock", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "tsugajunkie", "author_name": "tsugajunkie z5 SE WI \u2671", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tsugajunkie", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "Cultivars not easily grown from cuttings are grafted.  If by \u201ddifferent understock\u201d you mean different from the cultivar, then yes, they are grafted on a compatible species or genus grown from seed. tj ETA- Abies firma is an understock used for cultivars of firs meant to be grown in warmer zones (zone 6 or warmer).  It is not hardy in colder regions and hardier species of fir are used there.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "plantkiller-il_5", "author_name": "plantkiller_il_5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/plantkiller-il_5", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "Remember , dwarf are a mutation of a species . the only way to reproduce them is rooted cuttings  ( in which case , they would be on their own roots) or grafting on compatible root stock of mass produced seedlings ron", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "ken-adrian", "author_name": "ken_adrian Adrian MI cold Z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ken-adrian", "date": "2022-03-18", "text": "the mutations are usually inherently weaker ... and to get them a bit more vigor.. they are grafted onto more vibrant understock ... any tissue color away from green is weaker in the sense that it doesnt photosynthesize as green would .... and when your talking about a plant that might be a foot or 2 big in 10 yeas.. if half your tissue is white.. or yellow.. then one reason you have a reduced annual growth rate .. is because of such ... when you back up to the a species ... you can .. well the growers can ... root seedlings of the common species in bulk.. by the hundreds or thousands .. to use as grafting material for the odd balls ... and if it took ten years to get that foot or two big ... you arent going to have a lot of material you can graft .. it might be 10 or 20 years before the plant can come to market .... ken", "images": []}}

title: Help! Re-occurring Chlorosis! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "matthew-laplante34", "author_name": "ML", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/matthew-laplante34", "date": "2022-03-17", "text": "I'd overfertilized my plants several months ago. Most responded well to it. Others were a very different story. They appeared to really improve and chlorosis hit again, despite the plants not being fertilized. I'd leach again and change the plants' soil. It'd occur again and I'd leach again.The question becomes is this due to overfertilizing or nitrogen deficiency? My wife brought up a good point by pointing out that the grow lights are on for much of the day when the plants are supposed to be dormant. I'd foolishly set up the light timings to those used in a certain plant. A banana plant is also experiencing this. It goes through the same cycle. First though, clay pots offer plants a better opportunity to realize a greater measure of their genetic potential when measured against plastic pots or other pots with walls made of materials that are not gas permeable. This, because they offer significantly better gas exchange between gasses in the rhizosphere and the air surrounding the pot. Where applicable, the increased amount of evaporative cooling they offer also makes them passive root coolers when pots are exposed to direct sun or high ambient temps. The increase in evaporative water loss is a major contribution to decreasing the interval that perched water remains in grow media, limiting root function and health. Any patina of dissolved solids which occur on the outer wall of the pot are not in the soil solution, so are not available for uptake, and represent no threat to the plant. These dissolved solids pull water outward from the grow medium by the same mechanism curing salts 'pull' moisture from ham/ bacon/ sausage. What medium have you chosen as home for your plants' roots? What do you use as a fertilizer and how/ how often do you use it? Are you using any other products like tonics, insecticides, sprayed-on topical products of any kind? How do you make the determination it's time to water? BTW - I agree with Rhizo in that the solution is not going to improve if you add more P than the plant is capable of using. That scenario has no potential to be beneficial, only potential to be limiting. Excess P in the soil solution limits uptake of several nutrients (called an antagonistic deficiency), namely potassium, calcium, iron, copper, and zinc, some of which cause chlorosis. Also, the idea that nitrogen is \"for foliage\", P is \"for roots\", and K is for the plant's well being (often remembered by the phrase (up, down, all around) is misleading to the point of being pernicious. All 12 nutrients plants absorb by the root pathway are essential to the normal growth of every plant organ; and, you'll find that tissue analysis reveals very little deviation in the % of nutrients in the various organs of any individual plant. IOW, the leaves, roots, and stems that make up plant A will all have roughly the same level of nutrients in all 3 types of tissue. As it applies to conventional container culture, you would do yourself a favor if you can resist being drawn into the trap of dosing your plants with compounds aimed specifically at providing one or only a few nutrients. One of the major goals of fertilizing containerized plants is to make sure ALL essential nutrients are in the medium and available for uptake, at a ratio that mimics the ratio at which the nutrients are used, as closely as possible. Sunlight, with the sun straight overhead, is 100,000 lumens/square meter. The sun usually isn't straight overhead, so the sunlight we really get is more like 40,000 lumens/meter. Your Grossyland 2000W light (it's really not 2000W, but rather 2000W incandescent-equivalent, or 400 real electrical watts ) puts out something like  35,000 lumens. So, shining on one square meter (which is somewhat larger than the lamp itself), is something like the average sun. One foot above the plants, the 20x20 inch lamp is probably lighting up maybe two square meters. So  you're illuminating that area with about one half of average sunlight. That being the case, it you want to shoot for the equivalent of 8 hours of average sunlight per day, you could probably leave your lamp on for twice that per day. title: Constructing a Base for Retaining Wall Blocks for Small Raised Bed | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2022-03-18", "text": "I have a corner area of a garden where we want to build a raised bed as high, as we can get it, in a very limited space.   On the side closest to the camera in the photo, we have a cemented paver platform to hold back the new soil.    On the hedge side, we want to install retaining wall blocks two to three blocks high.   The raised mound is NOT on the plant side of the wall.  The raised mound is on the side of the wall closest to the camera.  That is why you are seeing the backside of the blocks.  That is where the new soil will be pressing. The retaining wall blocks need a good construction base so that they can be leveled and stay level.   The initial plan was to dig a ditch four inches deep, then line that ditch with landscape fabric, and then use about two inches of 1/4 inch gravel as the base.    Each block weighs about 25 pounds and is less than 12 inches wide.   So even with three of these stacked, we only need to support less than 100 pounds of weight over a 12-inch section.   That said, two inches is not much depth for a base. What is the best way to construct this base?   How many inches deep should the trench be?   How many inches of 1/4-inch gravel before we lay down the blocks?  How many inches of 1/4-inch gravel on the sides of the block as we come up to ground level?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/92c2949e0236cf3b_9169-w500-h279-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-03-19", "text": "1) Since retaining wall blocks are seldom, if ever, used in house construction, this is certainly a landscaping question. 2) The blocks are most definitely backwards. The rounded side is the face and the crease showing is the interlocking feature that should be against the soil. The blocks should also fit snuggly together around the curve so that there are no obvious gaps showing on the face of the wall. Any gaps will be in the back  to form the arc and are then filled by the soil. 3) If the standard 6\" height, this is barely a retaining wall at all and more of just a tallish edging system. Don't try to over-engineer it. A 2-4 inch gravel base trench is fine but the first course should be at least half way below grade. If the finished height is less than 24\", the wall really doesn't require anything more than to be back filled, but if it makes you feel better you can backfill immediately behind the wall with more gravel before filling in with soil. If the interlocking features are addressed properly, that wall is not going anywhere with the modest soil weight behind it.", "images": []}}

title: How I have eliminated Oil-based Polyurethane smell... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "dee-brown311", "author_name": "dee_brown311", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dee-brown311", "date": "2022-03-19", "text": "A quick side note, I am shocked that polyurethane brands, specifically Minwax, does not offer more of a warning about the longevity of \"off-gassing.\" It is understandable to deal with a toxic smell during application and sometime after, but the lack of education/honesty about their product, to me is complete negligence. Especially when these brands are carried at DIY home improvement stores and are bought by \"everyday homeowners\" and not restricted to just professionals. To sum up my situation... I bought my house in June 2021. I immediately sanded and refinished my floors in the Minwax stain and Minwax fast drying polyurethane for INTERIOR use. I did one coat stain, 2 coats poly. I aired out my house for an entire month before moving in July. As everyone can assume, the smell as intense, a 10/10! When we moved in a month later, I would rate it an 8/10. I cannot stress this enough for people thinking about using poly....DONT USE OIL-BASED POLY! The off-gassing is very real! All of your area rugs, your couch and soft fabrics will most definitely absorb the smell. And if you're like me, you will be washing/ cleaning constantly to get rid of it. I have always had a very fresh smelling home, and this \"adventure\" has consumed me for the past 6 months and has continued today. Today, I would rate the smell a 2/10. I ask everyone that comes into my house to rate the poly smell...yes, I'm that person. For those dealing with this, here are the methods I used: 1) AIR OUT YOUR HOUSE EVERYDAY! This is the most important. Create airflow by pulling air in and pushing air out using window box fans. I did this for 4 months straight. No Joke! Every room with 2 windows has an in and out fan. 2) I CLEANED MY FLOORS AT LEAST 4X A WEEK! I used my Shark floor steamer. I would fill a bottle with vinegar water and pour it on the floor, then go over with my steamer. I would repeat this with bleach water. This definitely helped neutralize the smell. I started this 1 week after the last poly coat. 3) AIR PURIFIERS! I used multiple methods, so not sure what has had the most effect. I have 2 CARBON FIBER air purifiers, which I leave on every day and turn the setting up on high at night. Carbon fiber absorbs VOCs. I also bought Activated charcoal fiber pellets and put them in mesh bags in closets and under furniture. Be sure you activate the charcoal by laying them in the sun for a few hours. Not sure if it actually works, but that's what I read. I have 2 Filtrete Smart Furnace filters which i taped to 2 box fans and let them run in the house as well. Air filters are expensive, and this does the same thing. This specific filter absorbs VOCs. These became very very black from absorbing the fine particles and worked awesome. Filter link: https://www.lowes.com/pd/Filtrete-Common-20-in-x-25-in-x-1-in-Actual-24-72-in-x-19-72-in-x-1-13-in-Electrostatic-Pleated-Air-Filter/1000420751 I use a Berger Lamp ever so often and also would put baking soda and water in a small crockpot to neutralize the air. Please change your furnace filter often during this process. I went through 3 in 6 months. Filter link: https://www.lowes.com/pd/Filtrete-2-Pack-1085-MPR-Micro-Allergen-Extra-Common-20-in-x-20-in-x-1-in-Actual-19-6-in-x-19-6-in-x-0-8125-in-Electrostatic-Pleated-Air-Filter/3123821 4) WASH SOFT FABRICS AND FRESHEN AREA RUGS! It's important to wash any fabrics taht have been exposed to the poly smell. I have consistently washed curtains, couch pillows/blankets, clothes and bedding during the \"off-gassing\" process. I have most of my clothes and off-season items in totes to avoid the exposure. I spray fabrics that i cannot wash with a backing soda/ vinegar/ eucalyptus mixture. The area rugs that I do have down, I have been freshening up every month or 2 with a similar backing soda/ vinegar mixture in my carpet cleaner. Even sprinkling backing soda on your rugs and let it sit before vacuuming can be helpful. 5) USE CANDLES, WALL SCENTS, ETC... These can be helpful but the last thing you want to do is mask/mix these smells with poly. Your goal is to really purify and clean the air. Poly has a sort of \"warm\" smell so i stayed away from \"warmer\" smelling scents like vanilla or sugar. I found that fresh, minty smells did better. Eucalyptus, Spearmint, Solar Musk, Citrus, Herb and Floral smells worked best for me. 6) OZONE MACHINE If you use one of these, definitely do your research on how to properly run one. Not sure if it helped much with neutralizing the floor smell, but it did help neutralize fabric smells. These machines work amazing and can make a dent in the \"off-gassing\" smell. I used it weekly the first couple months. FYI: don't put them directly on the floor, I set it on a stool. It can leave a mark, so I'm told. Again, these can be harmful so do your researched! There may be other things I'm forgetting. I tried to simplify this while giving as much info as possible. I am glad to see the off gassing is coming to an end...hopefully and I can actually feel comfortable having people over. I will never use poly again on a project of this scale. Hope this helped someone! :)", "images": []}

It also reduces the potentiality of the entire propagule collapsing by way of the leaf being shed if roots are unable to keep abreast of water requirements. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-03-19", "text": "Your friend is pulling your leg :-) But maybe not intentionally. Severe root congestion causes what is often called \"the poodle or pompon look\" the most conspicuous symptoms of which are concentrations of foliage immediately proximal to vine apical meristems/ apices, which are found at branch/ vine/ runner ends, and the function of which is to generate extension growth. Included as additional visual clues, would be markedly slowed extension growth, shorter and shorter internodes as the root congestion progresses, and diminishment of that glow of vitality we all strive to achieve. It doesn't matter much how faithful one might be about trying to keep up with the plant's nutritional and moisture needs as they will not prevent or alleviate the limitations levied by tight roots. There are 2 ways to relieve the stress of tight roots. The most common is by potting up, which I'm sure you're familiar with. It consists of lifting the root/soil mass from pot A and situating it in a somewhat larger bot B, then filling around the bottom and perimeter of the root mass with fresh soil. This is a half measure and provides only a little improvement in vitality, growth rate, and possibly appearance. The reason I identify potting up as a half measure is because it ensures the stress of congested roots remains as a limiting factor interminably, or at least until a pair of human hands gets into the root mass to correct the congestion and the wayward roots it causes. A full repot, OTOH, consists of (usually) bare-rooting the plant, pruning the roots with a focus on removing the largest of roots not attached to the base of the root-to-shoot transition zone and other 'problem' roots (encircling/ girdling/ crossing/ damaged/ j-hooked roots, or roots growing straight up/ down, and roots growing back toward the center of the root mass. A full repot frees up space which fine roots, the ones that do all of the plant's heavy lifting, can colonize, and works to ensure all roots get their share of moisture and nutrients. My experience with mandavilla is limited to a few plants grown as individual specimens and a few included in mixed plantings. Those plants I over-wintered were kept quite dry on the floor of a cool basement in low light. I very quickly learned that if I was to expect the plants to perform well year after year, they would need to be repotted every spring (hibiscus, too). A plant with a badly congested root system is much like a runner with a degenerative muscle or nerve disease in the feet or lower legs. No matter how much Gatorade (s)he drinks or supplemental nutrition bars (s)he eats, the disease is going to limit performance - same with a plant and root congestion. A healthy root system is a prerequisite to any hope for a healthy plant. A normal part of Mandeville's morphology are the preformed root primordia at every node, which places them among the easiest of plants to root. I wouldn't use water to root cuttings as the roots which form in water are structured much differently that roots that form in a solid medium. Water roots are filled with an airy substance (aerenchyma) which allows oxygen essential to root function to diffuse through the specialized root tissue from plant parts above the water line. This can be a problem in transitioning from a liquid to a solid medium because roots which form in water are very brittle, so they break easily, and they are inefficient at absorbing water from a solid medium, so they often die while transitioning between media types. This represents wasted energy because the propagule, now in a solid medium, is often asked to generate a second set of roots when most of its energy reserves will have been spent on the first roots to form, so at a minimum, it increases the likelihood of propagule collapse due to low energy reserves. Too, rooting a cutting is a race to determine whether or not roots can form and make connection with the propagules existing vasculature before fungal or bacterial, or even abiotic pathogens clog the plumbing and make the connection impossible. Starting my journey consumer reports had wood pella windows as the gold standard for energy efficiency and quality. I was going to do double hung... and then, I spoke to interior designer who told me marvin casement is the only way to go. ... so I looked at marvin casement wood windows and while trying to decide what wood type Is the best I stumbled on reasons why Marvin's wood aluminum clad windows have problems with sweating, and metal spacers and seals may have sweating issues.So.. back to square one. I care about energy efficiency and quality of windows. My lady friend says it should be wood because wood looks better... but what I really care about is energy efficiency and quality.Suggestions?Edit: I'm in Chicago land", "images": []}

Or was that another marketing ploy? If the aluminum cladding is roll-formed (Pella, Jeld-Wen, others), then there is that possibility. If the aluminum cladding is extruded (Marvin, Kolbe, others), then I wouldn't worry about it at all. Also, what type of wood should be used if I go with wood? Marvin has an abundance of choices. Lastly if I did decide vinyl, do you have a brand that you think is more quality than others? I wouldn't argue with any of the choices given in previous posts, with the caveat that the companies mentioned do offer different lines with different levels of quality and performance. But in energy performance comparison, even the lower lines are pretty good compared with other options. title: Cancer really does stink, feel free to skip | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "maddielee49", "author_name": "maddielee", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/maddielee49", "date": "2022-03-20", "text": "My reason for sharing my story  may be so people understand how sneaky and shocking cancer works.  I had zero symptoms, have always been healthy and active.  Not a clue what was going on inside of me.  Of course, I\u2019ve known people who have had cancer, thankfully most have fully recovered.  I hope to join them in total recovery, but am sad that so many others have gone through the pain and angst that the last month has brought me and those that love me. My husband and I have lived a very good life.  Married 52 years with few hiccups. Last November (2021) out of nowhere he got very sick - 3 weeks in the hospital , one week sedated on a vent.  (Sepsis) By the end of December he was home, with home health nurses, PT, OT and lots of support from family and friends. During his last PT appointment (early February) I mentioned to the therapist that I thought I might have a pulled muscle in my right thigh.  She knew my history of arthritis in the right knee and suggested I call my ORTHOPAEDIC surgeon if it got any worse.  We really thought I had just been more active, while caring for DH. After a few days I went to Urgent Care.   Doc agreed it was probably a pulled muscle.  Given meds and suggestion to rest as much as possible.  On Feb 14, DH took me to the ORTHOPAEDIC ER because the pain had gotten worse.  EXrays taken, bursitis diagnosed. By Saturday (2/19) I could barely move.  Our son got me to the ER where they were looking for an infection of the bursa\u2026.that day, an Interventional Radiologist was called in. No problem at all with the bursa. Femur fractured in 2 places. Fracture caused by a tumor that traveled from my lung to my hip area and basically exploded.  After a full body bone scan, a spot was also found on my brain.  Primary tumor is in the lung. (My Last cigarette was in the 1970s, people do wonder). Luckily, I was accepted as a patient at a renouned Cancer Center close to our home.  I was transferred to  H Lee Moffitt Cancer Center on March 1.  Total hip replacement done on March 3.  Up and walking on March 5.  Discharged to home on March 10.  Have been home with  PT, OT and nurses who come as scheduled. Numerous appts at Moffitt meeting teams of experts that I have great faith in. Hip surgeon wants the hip to heal before radiation.  Will know more after my 3/31 appt, but radiation of the hip area is expected. First radiation to the brain is on the 3/23\u2026.surgery may follow next week. Waiting for more info about the lung spot before treatment plan is decided. There really is very little pain with the hip replacement.  (the needle biopsy of the lung hurt more.)  I had heavy duty drugs while hospitalized before and after surgery.  I am now at the point that I save  a good  pill till I need it in the middle of the night.  Opiad constipation is another whole discussion, I\u2019ll spare the details. To say I am overwhelmed at times is putting things mildly.  We are blessed with wonderful family and friends that seem to know exactly what is helpful and what is not. Our 2 adult children have stepped up and taken care that DH and I at our numerous medical appointments with a list of questions and the calm mental state to listen to what our providers say. I never ask \u2018why me?\u2019 but I somehow wish I had more of a clue that something was going wrong inside me. I will never turn down a good thought, vibe or prayer.  Tell people you love that you really do love them.  Often. This forum still makes me smile most times.  I thought of you all when I had my 20 year old granddaughter go buy a recliner for me.
