title: Another miracle in the garden - | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jacqueline9ca", "author_name": "jacqueline9CA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jacqueline9ca", "date": "2022-03-20", "text": "Several years ago we lost our huge old 'Belle Portugaise', which had grown to about 20+ feet tall,  to some sort of gall on its roots. Ugh! Anyway, we had our gardener dig it up. Here is a pic just part of the top of it when it was blooming - it was much wider than this. Gave me a crick in my neck to look at it, but the blooms were one of the loveliest of all of my roses. I have seen BP in the gardens (or just unkempt lots) of many old old houses around our neighborhood - it is evidently a great survivor in our climate conditions.   About 3 years ago, when we heard that our town was going to pass a law making growing roses (or anything else) touching our house illegal, I started thinking about what roses I wanted to save. I was hoping we could move some of the most precious ones, but in case of accidents I started to root those, so I would have more than one plant. I said to myself that I should go find one of those old old BPs and root it too, but I never got around to it. All of my little \"trying to root\" cuttings - I had about 12, got put on our back porch, and our front porch, in 1  gallon plastic bags, and then in small pots under upside down small fish tanks as usual. Most of them just sat there, but did not die. As some of them did die, and I took other cuttings, eventually most of the labels I had put on them fell off or faded, and all of the pots got mixed up. One rose I really cared about rooting was Le Vesuve. I have 2 healthy plants of it growing happily in the garden which do not need to be moved, but a friend of mine really wanted one from my plants, which were from cuttings of an ancient huge one in our garden. In my experience LV has been way harder for me to root than other roses. So, I was very happy when it grew roots and made a small plant. I transplanted it into a larger pot, and then it gradually and very slowly got bigger. I was sending my friend photos of it as it grew. Actual years past, COVID happened, drought and water restrictions happened, and my rooted cuttings got sort of neglected. I had to re-do some of the cuttings (I am trying to root LV, Pax, Reve d'Or, and a few others), and they all got moved around. The furthest forward was my LV, although now it was just sort of sitting there. Last Fall I moved the LV, which was getting bigger again, into a VERY large pot, and put it in the sun where I had to pass it frequently, and could make sure it was getting water. About 6 months ago (our growing season here is 12 months, so the roses don't go dormant) it suddenly started putting out longer canes, and much larger leaves. Hmmm...it did not really look like LV. So, I decided to just let it grow, so I could find out which of the other roses I was rooting it really was, assuming that I had mixed it up. Two months ago I looked at it carefully, and its canes had leapt out of its pot, over the ner by tomato cage, and across the bed to a structure I have Colonial White (aka Sombreuil) growing on, as well as Cl Crimson Glory. As my eye followed the \"not LV\" canes, and untangled them mentally from the other roses, I realized they were 7-8 feet long! Definitely NOT LV! Very interested now in finding out who this was. Then in early Feb it started setting buds, and as they got bigger and bigger, and longer and longer, it hit me that they, and the leaves, looked like Belle Portugaise, but that was impossible. This was not a seedling planted by some bird - this was a cutting that I had planted myself. I thought and thought, and eventually remembered that right after BP died, which was at least a year before I started my mass (for me) rose rooting project, I did try to root BP, but it did not work. Ha! The first bud bloomed a couple of days ago - here is a picture of it:  Definitely IS Belle Portugaise, so somehow that cutting I tried to root survived, or made roots which survived my next rooting project, and it is now in its huge-but-not-big-enough pot, waiting to be planted in the new garden my DH made for me for our rose refugees! New growth appeared and it grew well last year. This winter of 2021-2022 was a near normal 8b with a few freezes into the teens and the rest in the 20s. Most importantly, there were no early warmups. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "hzdeleted-38632450", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-38632450", "date": "2022-03-22", "text": "You need mature plants to gather propagation material from. Realistically, you need to be thinking in terms of a 3-5 year timeline to get to a point where you're ready to roll and actually have a reliable volume of plants available. Or, you could find a wholesale nursery that propagates the varieties you want, who produces flats of rooted cuttings in trays of 32 or 72 which you can pot up and grow for a few months to make a saleable plant. The only shade that the yard does get is from the woody weeds that have grown into the back fence between my backyard neighbor and I (I've actually found that some of these weeds are mulberry trees, while the other was just a weed the size of a small tree). I assume the soil is bleached of all nutrients due to constant sun exposure and it being extremely sandy. The lawn is compact and so lumpy that it holds a lot water when the snow melts in the lower parts of yard, which drains/thaws into my garage causing ice to form around the garage, on the garage floor and on the driveway. The lawn is mostly dirt patches, weeds, and some turf. I believe the higher parts of the lawn had been caused by organic material building up from the mulberry trees and the woody weeds dropping their leaves because I can see on the other side of the chain link fence that my neighbors lawn is an inch or two lower than mine. I'm at a loss on what to do. I can't just add topsoil or sand to the low parts of the yard because then as the snow melts, it will melt into my garage more then what is already is. I'm thinking of rototilling it, grading it and adding nutrients back into the soil to ensure a fresh new start. I have a small budget due to the home needing major repairs as well so any suggestions would be appreciated! Thanks!", "images": []}

Where you live, any hard work like heavy pruning or repotting should be undertaken in early to mid-June, when recovery should be faster than at any other part of the growth cycle. It's much better that we recognize our plants have rhythms (search Circadian and endogenous rhythm) during which its level of vitality varies significantly, and to work in concert with these rhythms to make life easier for our plants, than it is to act on impulse and not reap the rewards of working with the plant instead of against it. title: Floof! Laundry! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "amylou321", "author_name": "amylou321", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/amylou321", "date": "2022-03-23", "text": "Do you have a designated place to fold/hang up your laundry when its clean? It was sort of a running joke in our home growing up that mom would ruin any fun thing we had by taking it over for her folding table. The ping-pong table we got for Christmas? Laundry folding table. The pool table that replaced it a few years later? Well, the felt got ruined because she used it to fold laundry on. And before I get scolded for not just doing my OWN laundry growing up rather than leaving my poor mother to slave away at it, my mother LOVES doing laundry. Do not know why, but she never let us do it ourselves, until we got old enough to actually NEED certain clothes at certain times, like for example, as a teen I only had 2 work uniform shirts and I needed them clean. She loved laundry, but was not an on call maid, So I started doing it myself when I needed it done. Otherwise, as I said, she really enjoyed it and still does. Weird. Now I believe she uses to giant chest freezer they keep in the laundry room to fold clothes on. I always dump the clean clothes on our bed and fold them there. I do laundry once a week usually. Including washing our sheets and comforter, its about 5 or 6 loads. I used to sit on the couch and fold them, making little piles all around me, but the bed has more room, so that is where I do it. Also, I hang up a lot of our clothes rather than fold them. We have a canopy bed, which makes it convenient to hang things on their hangers on until I am done processing the whole load of laundry and can go put everything away. Before I had to pile everything BACK in the basket to carry it back to the bedroom. Not a huge labor I admit, but the way I do it now is better. Where do you fold your laundry?", "images": []}

title: House vernacular: Home keeping, House Keeping, Cleaning, | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jan-moyer-pfvwus-pf~1384207622", "author_name": "JAN MOYER", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/jan-moyer-pfvwus-pf~1384207622", "date": "2022-03-23", "text": "What are the major differences in those terms, and why are they even important? First, they are only important as they relate to what I shall refer to as House Lust. Briefly, that is the obsession with all the common questions here on Houzz, My paint color, kitchen .....what about this backsplash ......is this good or bad, a problem, not a problem, and on and on. As designers, we are tasked with understanding a client, and understanding the life within any given home. Few things make us crazier than creating tailored to that client beauty and function, only to see it devolve. That \"devolve\" if you will, often stems from a lack of understanding of those terms above. It is baffling ( to me ) that for all the \"design agony\" that goes into any home or project, why does it so often seem to simply devolve? . Is it natural, can you avoid it, do you WANT to avoid it? Stop right here if you believe it's natural. Home Keeping: The structure. Do the things that are supposed to work every day, actually work? Your roof doesn't leak, all the toilets flush, your gutters aren't clogged, the windows open and close easily. Your front stoop isn't crumbling, and your basement is dry. That sort of thing. House Keeping: AHHHHH! Here she goes! Again. This is the daily keeping up. with things. The things from which nobody is spared, UNLESS you have an in home hired worker to follow you around,  Failure to understand this term, is to derive little long term, or even short term satisfaction from all your deign effort. It's laundry and its completion, its dishwasher loading and unloading. Counter top wipe downs. The act of restoring a basic level of order and cleanliness daily. Trash cans emptied and out the door, pillows fluffed, Toys stowed. Clothes hung/folded/stowed or in the laundry basket. Beds  made up , the quick fridge sort and wipe out before groceries bought. Meals prepared, eaten, and cleaned up post meal. House Keeping is All the small and ongoing messes of daily living , cleaned up/tidied up as they HAPPEN. It is an in the moment, within that day occurrence . The putting back of the out of place , \"where does this go, and why is is it HERE?!\" restore. It is now task, not \"later\" . For those obsessed with beauty? It extends to the styling and embellishing aspects beyond the basic. Fresh flowers, neatly folded and hung towels, ....A quick \"re org\" of a drawer, closet, pantry.. It is important to understand that this is different than ...........dreaded or not? Cleaning:  The deeper version of House Keeping. The weekly , or at least bi weekly event that gets to the real grunge. The dust, the dirt, the grime. Gunk off the faucets, tub, shower, spots off the mirrors. Floors  completely swept, mopped, carpeting and rugs vacuumed. Window sills dusted, blinds same. Sparkle restored to all the sinks. Sayonara to smudges and fingerprints. The level to which you do either of the above categories will vary by individual. You can do it yourself, or you can HIRE. The hire: Know this: There is no magic. No \"hire\" can truly make up for a lack of House Keeping. If you go this route, your results will be as good as the maintenance between cleanings. The person, the team....or you, will be in catch up mode. It will take longer. You will pay more. You will enjoy the fresh for a shorter period of time.....as the house devolves until the NEXT cleaning with failure to Keep House. More brutal truth? Circle back to the point. Your backsplash, your white shaker cabinets and new counter tops. Your paint color, and your rugs. .......your \"pops\" of color, and long sought and perfected lighting.....right down to your lovely new sofa, accent chairs and ALL OF THE REST? None of it will matter. NONE will shine in their brightest light. The designer whom you paid, your own inspo's and Instagram adventures, Pinterest Pins.....all of the EFFORT ?  Will appear to disappear in the devolve. Is this sad? Yes. Is it truth? Yes. Which is why I gave anyone who cares not, the \"stop here\" option: )", "images": []}

At least one, maybe more are asking the plant to deal with conditions it's not genetically programmed to deal with. This Overview should help you decide what needs tweaking. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source \u2013 photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water \u2013 so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16\u201d (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48\u201d (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. If you eliminate things like vaulted ceilings, can you more easily simplify away from all the hips and valleys? Or is it a much complex issue to solve? Trying to get a better understanding so I can articulate what we want and what we don't want! Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2022-03-23", "text": "A hip would be the type of roof shape. Valleys in roofs are usually created from the footprint of the building. A simple rectangle footprint could have no valley. A simple 'L' footprint could have 1 valley. An 'H' footprint could have 4 valleys, or none at all. If you are concerned with the look of many nested gables, porticos, dormers, and so forth, those can illustrate the footprint or be added to the simplest of roof shapes with nothing to do with the footprint. So anything and everything is possible in any scenario, limited only by your imagination and budget. An interior vault or cathedral ceiling, though affected by the roof layout, is not an overriding concern for the complexity of the roof or shape of footprint. You can have one with a simple roof or complex one. In general, the American vernacular has made an association with steeper roof slopes and more complex shapes and adornment to represent higher cost, quality, and design grandeur. However, these traits alone do not have to represent the term \"McMansion.\" The best way to articulate what you want is through pictures of examples to your design team.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2022-03-24", "text": "A common tool used with crushed granite bases for walkways and driveways is to use a geogrid under the rock and above the hard clay soil.   Geogrid is hard plastic screening with large openings.   Water easily passes through it.  Rocks get stuck into it and then the load of the rocks gets evenly spread across that grid.  Less of the rock sinks into the clay soil over time.   What I would like to know is where can I buy it in small amounts?   The typical minimum size I have found is 4 feet by 50 feet, and that is $90: https://www.amazon.com/My-Supply-Shed-Bi-Directional-Retaining/dp/B07DRPM2Q6 My application for this is to support a very low stone wall made of lichen boulders, like the ones in the photo below.    I simply want to make it harder for the stones to sink into the clay soil over time.  I will cut out a strip of the geogrid to run the length of the wall.    The wall is so low that it does not deserve the effort to build a base underneath it. P.S., if you want to create a stone border around something in your garden, you cannot go wrong with lichen boulders.  They are gorgeous and have a kaleidoscope of interesting colors.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ffe21867023be786_3115-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Has Spring sprung in your area? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "tinam1962", "author_name": "Tina Marie", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tinam1962", "date": "2022-03-24", "text": "Yesterday I met friends for lunch in one of the \"big city\" areas.  My little town is nestled between three cities.  Anyhoo, it was about a 40 minute drive for me and what a beautiful drive it was.   The further west I got, I noticed more and more dogwoods and redbuds starting to bloom.  Our dogwoods just have buds but not blooms.  It was a glorious day weather-wise and I drove back through one of the \"main drags\" of that city, which goes through an area of old homes, most with beautiful yards.  I decided not to hit one of the highways that would lead back to my little town and instead, took the backroads from a road that let me pass my old work place and the way I often came home.  So much greening out and blooming!  Sad thing is we are supposed to be very close to freezing Saturday and Sunday night.  It's good our dogwoods haven't bloomed out, maybe the blooms will be spared.  My tulip tree was in full bloom when we had snow/freeze a few weeks ago.  The next day, every single, beautiful bloom was brown.  : (   Our bradford pear blooms turned dirty looking.  Thankfully their leave are now coming out, so no more dirty blooms LOL.  My creeping phlox is starting to bloom, my candy tuft has been blooming for weeks, my tiny little quince bush has grown a bit and has blooms.  My hydrangeas are budding out and the new rhodies we recently bought have buds.  I can't wait to see them!!  The Mr. is building an arbor-type structure that will go out back and I have great plans for a climbing plant along with a large planter on at least one side.   I have a new blue nikko hydrangea on order and two clematis.  I bought a blue nikko last year, but it didn't survive the winter.  I love spring!  I even love our hot summers.  I just love having all the blooming trees and flowers.  We even have an annual Dogwood Festival here each April.  We have marked trails you can drive on and people on these trails go all out with their yards.  My favorite two trails are through area with gorgeous old homes.  I love to see all the yards, and get ideas on plantings.  Sorry, I am rambling, I know, but apparently I have SPRING FEVER!!  We are back in the 70's and will hit bottom this weekend - warming up again next week.  Spring is certainly temperamental in our area!", "images": []}

title: Doorbell Transformer Replacement | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-667833856", "author_name": "John A", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-667833856", "date": "2022-03-24", "text": "Hi, sorry for the novice question. I don't have electrical knowledge so trying to do a simple project and not sure what to do. Installed a google wired doorbell cam. when the doorbell is pressed it is not hitting the chime. Have read that it is likely due to the transformer not being powerful enough. I have bought a 24v transformer that I hope will work but the old transformer had three wires from one end: a green (tied to a bare copper wire) a black (tied to a double black wire) and a white (tied to a double white wire). The new one only has a black and white wire. What should I do? Also, there was a white wire coming out of the wall and connected to the chime FRONT terminal ... and red wire coming out of the wall connected to one end of the front of the transformer / the other end of that red wire to TRANS on the chime. Does it matter which red goes where on the transformer (one terminal on the front of it says LOAD above it, the other says NEC). Lastly, the google doorbell comes with a wire connecter (https://www.ebay.com/itm/333846312319?chn=ps&_trkparms=ispr%3D1&amdata=enc%3A1rq5nop_4S6iH_Xj57LDF1A96&norover=1&mkevt=1&mkrid=711-117182-37290-0&mkcid=2&itemid=333846312319&targetid=1599090335657&device=c&mktype=&googleloc=9010936&poi=&campaignid=15275224983&mkgroupid=131097072938&rlsatarget=pla-1599090335657&abcId=9300697&merchantid=101490060&gclid=CjwKCAjwrfCRBhAXEiwAnkmKmVlu8ljbgaUvffusbxlr1xB2e-PhnTN_vm9K9Z-xI3kSLM0N1PRXYhoCLpkQAvD_BwE). Should i use this and connected the incoming white and red to it (connecting the connecter open wires to the terminals only)? Or should i just ignore the 'insert' ends and just connect the wires to the terminals so it's two wires each on TRANS and FRONT? Thank you!!!!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "toxcrusadr", "author_name": "toxcrusadr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/toxcrusadr", "date": "2022-03-24", "text": "The green wire on the transformer is just a ground wire connected to the case of the transformer.   if the new transformer doesn't have a green wire, look for a screw terminal on it that may be painted green (NOT one of the two on the front which are the output terminals). Actually looking at the pics on ebay, there is a silver screw where the B&W wires come out of the transformer.  This is almost certainly for connecting a ground wire. The two front terminals on the transformer are the 'secondary' or output winding of the transformer. They are electrically equal (as opposed to the input wires where black is hot and white is neutral). LOAD means to hook up your chime to those terminals. Doesn't really matter which way. NEC is Natl Electrical Code. I'm not sure why that is there but it doesn't indicate that the terminal next to it is different from the other terminal. They're a handsome tree from this perspective, and the seeds aren't an aesthetic problem as they would be if the flowering ashes were, say, a street tree with nothing much else in the way of plants going on around them. The Rock, a largeish outcropping in one of the fields, has the largest laburnums I've ever seen, and come spring they bloom magnificently.  But I found out last year, which, like now, was blessed/cursed with a sunny spring, that the yellow clusters of blooms show up poorly against a bright blue sky.  The laburnums are on the top of the outcropping; they're big; I looked up at them perforce from below. I have two plants of this growing up trees in the woods at the edge of the shade garden. The three ramblers that have found their way up the two Leyland cypresses down in the big garden show to better effect. title: Site plans changed after signing, advice? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-815085161", "author_name": "HU-815085161", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-815085161", "date": "2022-03-25", "text": "Hello, we purchased our home in 2021 and a few months after signing the contract the builder changed the site plans. the units behind us were originally single story, then changed to two story. is there any recourse we can take as we feel we are not getting what we signed for.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "millworkman", "author_name": "millworkman", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/millworkman", "date": "2022-03-25", "text": "If he was legally allowed to chance from one story to two and did so thru the proper legal channel, then no there really is nothing you can do.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2022-03-25", "text": "Were you aware of the change before or after closing on the house? This question is a bit complicated.  If you became aware of the change after closing, it is possible that you have some recourse available, but it is not an easy or cheap position to argue and very likely isn't worth your time or effort. There is a concept known as promissory estoppel, where a promise or commitment was made by one party and the other party reasonably relied on that promise to take some action.  In your case, the question is going to be, did the original site plan constitute a promise or commitment? Was it presented to you without a disclaimer (e.g. subject to change)?  If so, you can argue that it formed the basis of your acceptance of the house and were damaged by the change (the damages are the easy part). Promissory estoppel is not usually a strong argument, but the particulars of a situation could make it fairly strong.  In reality, it is doubtful that you would recover attorney fees even if you did win, so it is not worth your time pursuing.  The most you are likely to get economically would be a privacy fence or some landscaping. Good luck", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-03-25", "text": "The proportions are by volume. I had planned on creating a large batch of the mix to use for various  pottings - is this advisable or should I proportion a mixture for each separate planting? How I approach things: As long as I have everything assembled and the Turface screened. I make several small batches such that the total volume made in any day-long session would be somewhere between 50-100 gallons, and I store them in 32 gallon heavy duty trash containers with wheels and keep an 18 gallon tub with rope handles ready at hand. The gritty mix is very easy to alter so it has more or less water retention. I make the 1:1:1 ratio in large quantities, then alter enough mix to suit an individual plant. While I almost always suggest any alteration should include more Turface MVP and less grit (for added water retention), or more grit and less Turface MVP for less water retention. Adjustments can as easily be made by simply adding a handful or two of one or the other to change water retention. Ideally, the bark fraction should remain at 1/3 of the mix, or less, to ensure the medium's structural integrity over the long term. The beauty in being able to use large particles of Turface MVP or grit to adjust water retention lies in the fact that aeration remains consistent and there is no need to suffer the consequences of relying on perched water to increase water retention. Water is still held on the surface of soil particles, in the internal pores of materials with open internal porosity, and at the interface where soil particles contact each other, leaving spaces between soil particles full of air from top of the soil column to the bottom of the pot. This results in a very healthy environment for roots, 'healthy roots' being an essential prerequisite to a healthy plant. Al", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~850907030", "author_name": "Lori Sawaya", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~850907030", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "Is it better to have the front door and the frame match in the wood stain You will find different points of view about this. IMO, exterior color serves the purpose of wayfinding. Especially important for a front door; It needs to clearly and quickly signal \"this is how you get in the house\". title: 'Treasure Trove' problems | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2022-03-25", "text": "For those who don't know it, 'Treasure Trove' is a huge rambler, a cross between 'Kiftsgate' and a garden rose.  I was just down looking at ours and wondering what to do about it.  We bought TT probably around 2004, planting it down in the shade garden and setting it to climb a mature black locust.  The rose got up to 30' or so and was a sight.  Then one night a high wind blew, and picture my surprise the next morning when I found no tree and no rose.  Well.  We had already built a small pergola-type structure to keep TT off our heads as we descended to that part of the garden, so we decided to extend the pergola and the steps below them, using the sawed-up trunk of the locust.  It was a reasonable solution, but the winter before last we got two feet of snow in three days, and that felled the pergola and the rose all over again.  (Actually, I think there might have been another collapse somewhere along the way:  the ice storm at the end of 2017?  It certainly did plenty of damage.) As a rule we build our pergolas of rebar, but this isn't working, even with a heavy weight of metal.  I was thinking of the steel tubing, square in cross-section, that DH used to build the pergola entrance to the shade garden and which hosts the double white Lady Banks.  Ha.  It's never fallen down.  However, the ground where the pergola is, or used to be, is a mixture of scree over rock, and steep, making setting steel posts in the ground, and construction in general, a difficult task.  DH is in his late eighties, too, and doubtfully up to this kind of job. So I ponder my great tangle of rose and wonder what to do.  I suppose I could just leave it as it is, but I would like to get back the pergola and the steps, and that route through the garden. title: Garden Armageddon -- Need Advice | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "laura-g_young", "author_name": "Laura (Z5a Fort Collins, Colorado)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/laura-g_young", "date": "2022-03-25", "text": "Hey everyone -- I wasn't on the forum much last season as my garden experienced what could be termed as The End of All Days. Let me explain. For nearly 20 years, I've lived in a small neighborhood that, up until recently, was bordered on three sides by horse pasture, alfalfa fields and a fallow, undeveloped area abundant in bluestem, rabbit brush and prickly pear. My yard, while very tiny, was one of the few in the area that A) had a decent variety of native plants and B) wasn't drenched in herbicides or pesticides. Then (surprise, surprise) all three areas got plowed under for condos and mini-mansions. So starting last summer, wave after wave of grasshoppers/Japanese beetles/voles/rabbits and other disturbed/displaced critters took refuge where...?  You guessed it. I got a handful of refugee toads and snakes as well, but they weren't enough to stop the onslaught. What the grasshoppers didn't nibble down to the nubble, the voles finished off this winter. Basically all of my perennials were dug up and gnawed into oblivion -- even my expensive serviceberry bushes that were finally starting to take off after three years. Weirder still, the voles even dug up and chewed through the entire rock garden, despite every effort to discourage them with live-trapping, cayenne pepper and other deterrants. All my ice plants, hens and chicks, etc. that I've gotten from you guys at the swaps....gone. (Click HERE to see grasshopper damage) The thing is, I'm not mad at the critters.  They did what they did to survive, not out of malice. That being said, I'm VERY sad that all my hard work over the last few years has been seemingly for nowt due to the imbalance due to this micro-upheaval (which I realize is nothing compared to what we humans are doing on a planetary scale.) So yeah.  I'm starting from scratch. All I got left is dead, rootless branches and dirt. I think it might be a good idea to just go with annuals for a couple years, until things balance out. Anyone else experience a complete wipe-out like this?  If so, what plants did you use during the recovery phase? --L", "images": []}

title: Present and future 1st world etiquette: plastic surgery | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2022-03-25", "text": "Time was that when people I knew had plastic surgery they would come back from a \"vacation\" and it was likely they would be tanned, and have new glasses and a would have done something different to their hair. Females and (at that time), particularly vain males. And everybody kind of pretended that nothing happened. I never knew anyone in my family who had plastic surgery. More recently, I feel like now there is a lead up, a discussion right before the event, opinions asked and so forth, and people openly have procedures done. And they often return to work pretty quickly. I should note that I work in an allied health field, and some of the work I do myself is cosmetic, and I could easily be certified to do botox and filler because of my background. So all of this may be a little bit more wide open in my daily circumstances. But in general I think people are way more upfront about it. I should say that I am not usually very \"pro\" plastic surgery and I am pretty much \"anti-\" filler and Botox. In my age group meh, go ahead but I know people in their 20s getting filler and Botox, and I am not convinced that there will not be problems with injecting a toxin (especially) repeatedly, subcutaneously, for the next who knows how many decades if you are starting at 30. One coworker has had really excellent work done, first bags under the eyes, and now a neck lift. But her surgeon does primarily corrective and reconstructive surgery (and does cosmetic to pay the bills), and he is very conservative and also does not raise expectations. It looks great and I told her it looks great. But when she got some Botox, I said \"Don't do that anymore, you don't look right\".  I have also told a couple other people, co-worker/professionally who have gotten Botox, \"Don't get it in this spot, next time\". I just can't say \"Yeah, great...\" if I don't think so. Anyway, two people in one workplace just came back fairly fresh from plastic surgery. One I am pretty friendly with. I can't really tell yet, because it's early but it's, I don't know, a pointy-eyed, at this point, and she said the same, but do you say \"Yeah, I think so, too\" because it's done. I feel like it may not necessarily be my place to agree, even if I do.  The other person--I think so far it looks horrendous, and I spent the entire day yesterday looking about 30-degrees off-center when I had to talk to her. I am just afraid at some point she is going to ask me point blank what I think (she's that kind of person) and I am going to have trouble being convincing that I think it looks good, I think. On the flip side of this is that most of these same people have pointed out what they think I could have done, mostly the bags under my eyes, and possibly a multiple scar correction because of scars around one eye which as I age is starting to make my eyelid droop when I am tired. So it's not like these things aren't presented to me as well. I won't do anything unless it presents a functional issue, mostly because I think most men look silly when they do anything around their eyelids. I'd rather have a droop than look like I had an eyelift. Anyway this is just rambling, but I think it is something that we may end up having to discuss with people after the fact, and it may not be easy to navigate. I am not sure there is a nice but non-committal response that applies here.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mntreegrower", "author_name": "mntreegrower", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mntreegrower", "date": "2022-04-17", "text": "Do you know what kind of serviceberry you have? Our architect prefers that we use a standard AIA builder contract. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2022-03-27", "text": "My 2 cents, (and yes I have said part of this many times before)... The right builder is much more important than the right contract and relatively few builders use the AIA contracts. The AIA contracts are great, but if I were a builder the very last thing I would want to do is use a contract that I am not intimately familiar with, especially given the current construction market.  I suspect most builders would decline the change unless there is some significant benefit to them.  However, if your builder sees this as an opportunity to be recommended by, and regularly work with, your architect, then they may be amenable to the AIA contract. I would not write off a good fit for a builder simply because they refuse to use the AIA contract.  I typically tell people to have the builder's contract reviewed by an attorney (in this case maybe an attorney and your architect) to spot the possible risks and conflicts and then work to mitigate those risks. ETA: The contract itself should govern conflicts not create them.  There is significant potential for the builder to proceed in the manner he is familiar with even if that conflicts with the new contract terms.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "meierfamily", "author_name": "Amanda Meier", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/meierfamily", "date": "2022-03-26", "text": "We bought a dining table on Facebook marketplace for cheap and had it refinished by a small local company. The table top is wood veneer. After it was refinished, we were told it was stained with a Varathane oil based stain, and then sprayed with 4 coats of Varathane Satin polyethylene \"for durability\". I can't find any information online about polyethylene finishes on wood - I'm not sure if the person meant polyurethane (the stain and finish info were sent in a text). We let our table fully cure and did not use it for 30 days after it was delivered. But since we have started to use it, every little thing is leaving stains and marks on the table. (not scratches, but things penetrating into the table very easily and leaving stains) The littlest bit of food or liquid that gets on the table leaves a stain that will not come out. Some of the stains I don't know how they even got there, but I know they weren't there when we got the table back from being refinished. I haven't tried much but a soapy microfiber cloth to remove the stains because I don't want to ruin the finish....but that didn't work and I'm not sure why this is happening. We have little kids and we expressed to the people doing the refinishing that we wanted a durable finish that could withstand some messes (obviously we know no finish is impenetrable). We use placemats under our kids' plates and we use coasters for drinks, but some food or water or oil from salad dressing getting on the table is inevitable. It is a dining room table, we eat here! And kids are messy! I really don't like table cloths and don't want to have to use one all the time just to keep my table looking nice. Plus they are also very inconvenient with kids as I'd pretty much have to wash it after every meal (not practical). Any thoughts on why this is happening and is there any way to clean it off without damaging the finish? Or are we just doomed to having to use a table cloth or having an ugly table with tons of marks and stains all over? title: Disappointed in Black Windows - Help | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-156614726", "author_name": "Marla", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-156614726", "date": "2022-03-26", "text": "Went to the local Home and Garden show yesterday and was very disappointed when we checked out the black on black windows \ud83d\ude2d. All the window manufacturers of vinyl black windows don\u2019t paint the inside edges where they would wear and tear so when you open them you see strips of white. Our only option is to go to wood frame and have the maintenance of painting or fibre glass that was up to 30% more $$.  Also looked at having grills inserted into glass and one manufacturers warranty gets cut in half as soon as you add grills and others kept same warranty but advised against grills due to higher fail rates.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/65e2c875023f14f7_1325-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~2047594802", "author_name": "HomeSealed Exteriors, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~2047594802", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "Interesting comments from consultants and designers. 1) Aluminum is not advisable unless it is in an appropriate climate (warm), or is necessitated by some other factor such as being in a high rise condo building or something of that nature. Yes it is \"thermally broken\", however the limits of that are generally tested and destroyed in a cold climate as aluminum is very conductive. 2) Vinyl windows (much like wood, fiberglass, and metal) come in a variety of designs, quality tiers, and perfromance levels. Stating that you don't like a material becasue of the design is like stating that you don't like hamburgers because you had a bad one at McDonalds, or perhaps more than one. This is admittedly a generalization on my part, but the extent of experience that many designers, consultants, architects, etc have with vinyl windows is of the \"dollar menu\", builder grade variety. As for the original concern, @Marla, you may notice that windows of various materials don't paint \"high friction\" areas for obvious reasons. Many fiberglass and wood products will have vinyl jamb liners of another color, and/or similarly unpainted areas. This is generally considered the \"guts\" of the window, where hardware, fasteners, and other items that make the window operate (and with little regard to the appearance) are located. It just so happens these areas are typcally white on a vinyl window, on wood or fiberglass they may be beige or brown. If that would make a difference, you could check with the manufacturer of your choice to see if they'd apply the black coating to a different color vinyl extrusion such as beige or brown. Some may paint all surfaces in and out of the jambs, but there are more that do not than those that do. Lastly, its very odd for the warranty to be affected by adding grids. The vast majority of manufacturers don't have anything like that in place, I'd look at other options regardless of the material that you ultimately choose.", "images": []}}

title: Need help saving a dying baby Serbian Spruce + 1 other question. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kevin-counter", "author_name": "Kevin Counter", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kevin-counter", "date": "2022-03-26", "text": "Our local landscaping place had 4 evergreen trees (1 white pine, 2 blue spruce, 1 Serbian spruce) leftover from last year, so we bought them for a discounted $75 (original price was $189). Right after we had them delivered, the winter struck and the ground was frozen for over a month here in Central PA. I did some online research and for spruce it said the best time to plant them was February. So I was holding out until then hoping the trees didn't die. Well, they didn't. I also could not break through the frozen ground even if I wanted to. Eventually Feb came and the ground was still frozen. I borrowed our neighbor's backhoe as a last ditch effort to get these trees in the ground. It took hours of work to break through the ice, but I eventually had 4 holes dug. I returned the backhoe and found my trees were frozen to the ground. I have never planted trees before, so this was all new. I eventually broke the trees free gently, but realized they were too heavy to move, even with my family out there all pitching in to help. I've read where they grow about a foot a year, so these have to be 4-6 years old by their size. They must weight hundreds of pounds. I was eventually able to maneuver the white pine onto a thick sheet of plywood, then rope the wood to my riding lawn mower and drag it over to its hole. It was a ton of work to just get that simple task done, and I am sure it probably did some subtle damage to my lawn mower. I didn't want to have to do this 3 more times. I noticed our Serbian spruce is now half brown/dead and half green. I knew I was losing one of these 4 trees. I borrowed my neighbors backhoe again and he brought it over last night. Someone else had been borrowing it for weeks. So here's my first question: can my Serbian spruce be saved by putting it into the ground finally? Or will it just continue to die? I don't want to waste the effort and time if it has no chance. But if there is a way to bring it back to life and turn all those brown needles green, I will do it today. My second question is I've seen mixed reviews over how to plant these trees. Many youtube tutorial vids just show them putting the tree in the ground and covering it with dirt. Others add all sorts of compost and other nutritious soils from the store. And yet others go into cutting the root ball at various angles before dropping it into the ground. Our trees are all wrapped in the canvas sack material with metal wiring holding it all together. Can I just clip through the metal wiring, remove the canvas sack, and drop the trees into the ground, then pile the dirt back around them? The guy who owns the landscape store told me you don't need to add anything special. Just add the dirt that was removed from the ground to make the hole. Is it really that easy?", "images": []}

We completed a remodel of a 100-year-old home last summer.  Interestingly, the kitchen sits over the garage and the subfloor of the kitchen/ceiling of the garage is a 5\" thick floating concrete slab.  Same slab approach they used in all the bathrooms. We wanted to install hardwoods (previously there was tile).  The vendor found a 1/4\" thick glue-down oak product with the same narrow width as the original oak floors throughout the remainder of the home.  I'm honestly not exactly sure of the terminology, but I believe it is an \"engineered\" product, but not like a laminate (they installed each individual board, then sanded and stained like a nail-down product).  They glued the wood directly to the concrete rather than putting down a plywood subfloor as they didn't want to create large step-up transitions with the adjoining rooms. Well, about 6-9 months after install we started getting significant cupping.  Then, we started getting multiple soft spots where the hardwood would compress/pop when you stepped on it.  The main contractor and the flooring subcontractor said they see this all the time, and they would just use the Dri-Tac wood repair system.  No problem. They drilled holes, injected the Dri-Tac glue (they had to inject A LOT of glue), and then told us to stay off the floors for 24 hours.  When we came back 24 hours later, however, all of the areas they glued had popped up.  Some of the boards were now \"only\" 1/8 inch higher than the surrounding, non-repaired boards, but some were 5/8\" higher.  See attached photos. The contractor and flooring sub said this was just temporary because the glue has water in it and that the floors would settle back down to normal after 24-48 more hours of drying.  One week later, they haven't budged. So now we have multiple significantly raised areas in the middle of our floor.  The contractors initially said they could just sand them back down, but how do you sand 5/8\" of elevation on a 1/4\" board? Has anyone ever seen this with the DriTac product (the label does say some temporary cupping can occur)? Any idea how to fix this? Any idea why the floors cupped/popped so soon after install and how to keep the rest of the flooring from doing this? So what has happened is your rootstock has overgrown the edible variety.  If you see any growth with monofoliate leaves, that is what is left of your edible variety (kumquat).  If not, then the edible variety has died out. Rootstock, if allowed to grow shoots, will often out-compete the edible variety. Many of the trifoliate hybrids used as rootstock are semi-deciduous. title: 1950's Bathroom wall construction, plaster over cement over drywall | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "allen-hayden17", "author_name": "Allen Hayden", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/allen-hayden17", "date": "2022-03-26", "text": "My house was built in 1954 and has bathrooms that are (on all side) a thin layer of 1/16-1/8 white plaster, over what looks like about 1/2 inch of plaster / grey cement (?), over a 1/2 inch of drywall nailed to the studs. Can anyone school me on the terminology for this build method so I can research in depth? I want to DIY repair the damage I have along the walls behind where a sink and cabinet used to be without having the replace the entire wall to the ceiling. The drain vent pipe from the sink busted and allowed moister into the wall and the wall started \"puffing\" in areas (it was soft and crumbly to the touch, so it's got to go). I have demoed it in sections and wish to replace the sections as needed. Also the floor has about 2 inches of poured cement over the baseboards instead of (what I expected to find) plywood sheets. The floor had linoleum over 4 inch square tiles that came up as soon as I started pulling the linoleum up. Where the previously mentioned sink and cabinets were (which will be replaced with new), there is no cement, so I'll have to fill that in and then want to lay new larger 10 - 12 inch tiles.     Thanks for any info you are able to provide.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2292175a023f92f7_3616-w500-h333-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a12210aa023f92f8_3617-w500-h333-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "cathyryankoch", "author_name": "Izzy Mn", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cathyryankoch", "date": "2022-03-27", "text": "My sister and BIL bought a house built in the 1950's. It had some unusual drywall, very hard. Found out it's called rock lath, may go by some other names. It has three layers to it. First what seems typical drywall, on that a thin layer of what appears to be cement like coat (about 1/8\"), then a very thin coat of plaster on the finished surface.  Like I said it's very hard but it does seem to make for a very quiet house. The tile work in their house is similar to yours and of how they were done back then. Tile was laid into a bed of concrete/cement ( or whatever the proper name)  The tile work was in good condition in their home. They were going to tear it out (they are very good at doing remodeling and even built their own house) but someone suggested that the old tile is now a desired thing for some so they left it. They were also warned removing the old tile from floors and walls takes a sledgehammer because it's all set in a thick bed of mortar (I think that's the correct word) Your tile on the floor is obviously messed up. You will probably have to chisel it all out and build up the floor to proper height to lay new tile or whatever flooring you decide on. Edited..I see down stream someone said that the cement like layer is brown. My sister's had a gray cement color. Probably similar, just done a little different.  My bil added more outlets and had a heck of a time cutting holes. He also removed a small, two feet, portion of a wall, he said it was a real pain and had to purchase blades for cutting concrete because what he usually used wouldn't work at all.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2022-03-27", "text": "It's rock lath (gypsum board almost like drywall) +brown coat + finish coat plaster.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "jeff-meeks", "author_name": "Jeff Meeks", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jeff-meeks", "date": "2022-03-27", "text": "I had a similar construction method in my bathroom walls...tar paper and metal lath attached to the studs and then mortar \"floated\" onto the wall and a final finish coat of plaster. It makes for a very solid wall and was a beast to demo. Where I live for all walls except inside a shower the common practice is to use blueboard and apply a coat of finish plaster. In my shower I wanted to paint the ceiling as so when  with a 3 mil vapor barrier, cement board and then veneer plaster. Ask over a johnbridge.com as well. They will be able to recommend the materials you should use to patch your walls. But veneer plastering takes a lot of skill.", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "md7112", "author_name": "Mike", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/md7112", "date": "2022-03-30", "text": "For the walls, rock lath is the correct answer. In my house, two layers of gypsum panels (the precursor to today's drywall) topped with a finish coat of plaster. Rock solid. Doesn't ding. Great sound insulation. Pain to demo/patch/cut holes in. Thickness in my house is 7/8\"-- I usually make 3/8\" wood furring strips and then fasten 1/2\" drywall to that. You could also use 3/8\" drywall on top of 1/2\" drywall. If you're using any power tools to cut it, the poster above is correct, you'll need carbide or diamond tipped for the top layer plaster. It will ruin regular metal blades. That said, a regular drywall hand saw and a little elbow grease will get you right through it too (just requires more effort than cutting regular drywall). Regarding your baseboards, that is because there had been tile there. These bathrooms are mud bed construction. There are boards between the joists that are flush with them and form a subfloor, then tar paper, then wire mesh, then 1.25\" of concrete. You can tile right over it and fill the hole with regular concrete. You can also tear it out and do a new subfloor if you have concerns about height, but that requires mores sweat and a couple trips to the dump. Just a sledgehammer and pry bar will get the job done, but use as light a touch as possible, or you will crack the plaster in surrounding rooms.", "images": []}}

On the heat, moisture, and etc. issues with the combos, that's the result of their using condenser drying mechanisms for the ventless drying.  The good news on a stacked set is that several brands of compact washers & dryers now offer dryers using heat-pumps which don't put much heat or moisture into the laundry space. title: Small home privacy | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "sadiebabe", "author_name": "Sara Davis", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sadiebabe", "date": "2022-03-27", "text": "Our new to us home was built in the 40's. The hall from the dining room is the link to two bedrooms, a full bath, the kitchen and the basement. The house was updated at some point in the past 20 years and the doors to the bedrooms and bath were all replaced. The issue is that there is no sound privacy from the bath or bedrooms. What kinds of doors could help with this?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "blazedog37", "author_name": "Helen", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/blazedog37", "date": "2022-03-27", "text": "Solid doors are generally fairly soundproof but nothing is going to be 100% so you would also need to use other soundproofing techniques depending on how sensitive you are and what the issue is. I had cheap hollow doors which I replaced with solid doors and the lower sound is noticeable when I close a door. Fabric, rugs and upholstered furniture absorb sound. White noise machines help if the issue is someone being disturbed by sound coming from the hall or anoth room. Acoustic material cam be applied to walls or even into walls.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "artemis78", "author_name": "artemis78", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/artemis78", "date": "2022-03-29", "text": "We have a house with a similar design, it sounds like, except a couple of decades older. Our house still has its original solid wood doors and when they're closed, they do a very good job of buffering sound. (When they're ajar, as my kids are constantly leaving them, it makes a huge difference in what you hear.) If you have hollow core doors, swapping them to solid wood would likely make a big difference. ETA: Also, probably a bigger project than you're looking for, but we are doing work right now with some walls along our bedroom open, and are taking the opportunity to add insulation even though they're interior walls. No idea how much this will help, but it can't hurt!", "images": []}}

title: Stung by a wasp/carpenter bee type while emptying out pots | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "getgoing100-7b_nj", "author_name": "getgoing100_7b_nj", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/getgoing100-7b_nj", "date": "2022-03-27", "text": "I was just emptying out pots brought in from outdoors where the plants have died for some reason or another. Not wearing any gloves... and felt a sharp pain in the middle of two fingers, thought it was wayward splintered wood ... no sign of wood and then saw the culprit in the potting mix. Still feeling the sting, can't see any stinger, using cold compress and keeping fingers crossed. How do you avoid such a mishap?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "Like rhizo, I have also been a professional horticulturist for many years. But unlike rhizo, I have been stung multiple times :-)) Sometimes it is unavoidable......sometimes not. The bee stings were my fault. Early with my first real garden, I was wandering the yard barefoot and stepped on a bee. Can't blame it for striking back! The second bee sting happened when a bee flew in/got caught in the top of my wellies and couldn't find its way out. I am not sensitive or allergic so no big deal. The major sting incident was not my fault. I was working on weeding a bed and pruning back a huge rose. The bed included a birdhouse on a tall pole. Unbeknownst to me, wasps had taken up residence in the birdhouse and took offense to me being in their territory and so close to the nest. When I heard the buzzing, I looked up but it was too late. I was attacked by the wasps and received at least 7 stings......on my head!! My scalp felt like it was on fire and I have never had quite so severe a headache! But ibuprofen, an ice pack and a rest, and I was good to go in a couple of hours. For a single sting, aloe verde or Benadryl applied to the sting as soon as possible will soothe and reduce any inflammation. Also cold or ice packs and an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen or aspirin can help. And if you have any adverse reaction, get to the ER or a doctor ASAP. btw, I took revenge on the wasps :-) The next evening at dusk, when they were all tucked away in their birdhouse squat, I nuked 'em with a long distance wasp spray! I also removed the birdhouse from the middle of my planting bed to discourage future colonies from setting up house. I have a very strong affinity for bees of all kinds and encourage them in my gardens. But I draw the line at wasps and hornets!!", "images": []}}

title: Piano lavabo bagno in rovere, dubbi verniciatura e resistenza | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "manuela-amoroso", "author_name": "Margherita", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/manuela-amoroso", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "Buongiorno a tutti, un amico di mio marito che lavora il legno ci ha proposto un piano lavabo in legno massello di rovere (su cui andrebbe poggiata una ciotola e un rubinetto) che andrebbe a trattare con vernice all'acqua, dicendoci comunque di asciugare sempre perch\u00e9 l'acqua farebbe rilasciare tannini al rovere facendolo diventare grigio( e non ci sarebbe poi nulla da fare). Ora, senza sapere leggere e scrivere, mi chiedo. Uno, non si potrebbe usare un'altra vernice pi\u00f9 resistente? (a quanto pare lui usa solo quell'acqua). Due, potrebbe essere pi\u00f9 adatta un'altra essenza di legno? Tre, attorno alla ciotola, sulla base intendo, e attorno al rubinetto, non ristagnerebbe comunque acqua? Un architetto a casa di una nostra amica ha fatto mettere una lastra di gres larga quanto la ciotola, e dello stesso colore bianco, poggiata a sua volta sopra il top. Vi sembra un'idea interessante? Lavabo e rubinetto gi\u00e0 l\u00ec abbiamo, si tratta solo di scegliere il piano. Grazie a chi vorr\u00e0 darmi un parere.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "architetto-marco-finardi-alma-group-pfvwit-pf~917408256", "author_name": "Architetto Marco Finardi - ALMA GROUP", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/architects-and-building-designers/architetto-marco-finardi-alma-group-pfvwit-pf~917408256", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "Ciao Margherita, innanzitutto la verniciatura all'acqua \u00e8 sufficientemente resistente ma il problema, come scrivi tu, \u00e8 il tempo. Il ristagno inevitabile dell'acqua alla base della ciotola provocher\u00e0 quasi sicuramente un'alterazione della superficie del legno. Questa, anche se non dovesse portare a deterioramento, provocher\u00e0 comunque una pessima alterazione dei colori da sembrare sporco o degradato. Io ti sconsiglio di poggiare direttamente sul legno il lavabo. La soluzione di utilizzare una lastra di gres non mi entusiasma, preferirei utilizzare una lastra di rame (o lastra metallica con finitura rame) che sbordi leggermente dal lavabo ma, comunque, potrebbe portare al ristagno d'acqua sotto la sua superficie.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "manuela-amoroso", "author_name": "Margherita", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/manuela-amoroso", "date": "2022-04-05", "text": "Architetto grazie del consiglio prima di tutto. Sono pi\u00f9 tranquilla sulla resistenza della verniciatura, certo capisco anche il problema del degrado sulla base lavabo. Pensando a suo tempo proprio a questo abbiamo scelto un lavabo ovale con bordo quasi dritti (se rendo l'idea) di modo tale che sia facile asciugare tutto intorno (rispetto ad esempio a un modello pi\u00f9 a ciotola con base piccola e molto svasata come l'abbiamo adesso che secondo me \u00e8 pi\u00f9 scomoda per l'intento). Effettivamente qualunque materiale venga posto fra lavabo e legno avrebbe lo stesso risultato del degrado sui bordi se capisco bene. Mi sa che a questo punto conviene scegliere ci\u00f2 che piace e, che dire, quanto dura dura! \ud83d\ude05\ud83d\ude05", "images": []}}

title: Woah! Slow down on the composting. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kennesaw50", "author_name": "General", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kennesaw50", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "There is a widespread misunderstanding that the final product of composting, \u201chumus\u201d, is stable. In fact, humas continuously decomposes over a period of years. That is why more compost is added to the garden every year. That is why no-till practices, which reduce the amount of oxygen available in the soil reduces the breakdown of humus and other organic matter in the soil. That is why top soil is typically less that a foot deep in many parts of the country, even after many thousands of years of organic material naturally being added. Only in areas with very cold soil, such as Alaska, very acid soils, such as peat bogs, or very low oxygen levels (swamps/bogs) does the slow decomposition of organic matter result in the deep buildup of humus and organic material. (Peat bogs can become several hundred feet deep over many thousands of years.) I recommend that when practicable, composting be done by incorporating the raw organic materials into the soil or used as a mulch. The organic material will decompose slowly and release nutrients over a longer period of time, and the soil will maintain a higher percentage of organic material. With respect to seed or disease issues, incorporating the organic material into the soil will resolve many insect issues. If the garden plant residue is diseased, the soil will already contain diseased residue from disease spores from dropped leaves, remaining roots etc. . Crop rotation is an effective defense against soil-borne disease.", "images": []}

title: Overwintering a few annuals in a cold cellar and now it is spring | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rouge21-gw", "author_name": "rouge21_gw (CDN Z5b/6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rouge21-gw", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "For the first time last Fall I brought in a lantana and a vermillionaire (cuphea hybrid) and a geranium into our cold cellar, all in their pots. This location got to probably a low of 3 or maybe 2 celcius (36/37 F). I brought up the lantana first, cut it back, sited it the warmth and sun of a south facing window. I had it there for 3 weeks w/o any sign of life :(. (Our dahlia was in the same location and it has shown life 15 days after being brought up) I have just brought up the cuphea hybrid into the indoor warmth, near the sunny window...fingers crossed. I am just curious if others have successfully overwintered lantana or cuphea in the way that I have described.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-03-28", "text": "The cuphea is hardier than you might expect. This past December we experienced a week of really cold weather....got down to about 25F (-4C) and never got above freezing for most of that time. The cuphea looks very dead at the moment and I fear a whole week of severe cold (and snow and ice) was far too much for it. It really does need some heat to kick into life again and as much sun as you can muster but I think it should be fine. Just don't expect a fast recovery :-) As an aside, I have NO room to overwinter anything iffy indoors so any temperennials I grow have to be able to withstand a PNW winter outside. title: Interior designer dilemmas... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "katy3816", "author_name": "katy3816", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/katy3816", "date": "2022-03-29", "text": "Delete", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~92364733", "author_name": "Kristin Petro Interiors, Inc.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~92364733", "date": "2022-03-29", "text": "I can understand your frustration.  With this extremely busy market, I am also limiting my jobs to new construction or whole-house remodels.  It can be difficult to manage a lot of smaller jobs so many designers are focusing on fewer larger jobs.  Another reason is that remodeling is very challenging right now with the supply chain issues.  With some appliances taking up to a year, it can be very difficult to schedule contractors so far out.  And then you have to order and store everything else very far in advance to avoid major price increases.  New construction builds have a much longer timeline so they are a little easier to manage right now. My advice is to be very flexible with your timeline.  If you tell a designer you want it started or done by a certain date, they may not want to take the risk of your job not finishing on time.  Be prepared that a remodel you plan for this year may not start production until next year. Also, a designer may have architectural or structural engineer resources for your ceiling, so start with finding a designer who is experienced in construction design and hold off on contacting architects on your own. Finally, do not get too hung up on finding a designer who has the look you want in their profile.  A good designer can create a variety of styles and it could be they just haven't completed or photographed one in the style you want.  Focus on their process when you talk with them.  A firm with multiple designers may also be better able to accommodate you.", "images": []}}

title: Roses you can’t grow and your substitutes. | Houzz Forum

I know most of us have been here: We can\u2019t convince our tender soulmate rose to thrive in our inhospitable zone, the rambling rose we deeply desire will instantly devour our inner city postage stamp lot and then move into our neighbors\u2019, our much coveted rose suckers wildly and we are already madly shoehorning plants into the last 3 inches of garden real estate, or the holy grail rose has been out of commerce for two centuries except possibly on a remote island in the heart of the Bermuda Triangle (postage and handling = life savings). Fortunately for us die hards, breeders are hard at work creating miraculous new cultivars to salve our hearts and satisfy our cravings. Some rose substitutes are so good that they make me feel like I\u2019m cheating the system somehow. Like eating my weight in chocolate without actually consuming the sugar and empty calories. These are some of my most satisfying substitutes. Would you like to share yours? Kim Rupert\u2019s delightful, lavender-purple, multiflora-like, cluster blooming \u2018Lauren\u2019 substituting for enormous \u2018Veilchenblau.\u2019 Alas, I finally surrendered this beloved purple rambler. I grew \u2018Veilchenblau\u2019 in my last garden on a triple lot. I have attempted to wedge \u2018Veilchenblau\u2019 into this one for 10 years in 10 different ways. My current garden is the size of a pea, and I am tired of digging up big roses and dragging them around in vain attempts to relocate them. \u2018Lauren\u2019 is a great fit! Kim Rupert\u2019s \u2018Purple Buttons\u2019 instead of \u2018Cardinal Hume\u2019. Size again. Kim Rupert likens the scent to Red Hots. I agree! Paul Barden\u2019s super gorgeous and super healthy \u2018Marianne\u2019 replacing lusciously fragrant but always diseased \u2018Abraham Darby\u2019 and fulfilling my cravings for \u2018Gloire de Dijon\u2019 with her impossible apricot decadence. Disease and climate. I am not a masochist. I will never grow Marechal Niel either. And speaking of Marechal Niel, I grow \u2018Buff Beauty\u2019 (Bentall, 1939) and Paul Barden\u2019s \u2018Jeri Jennings\u2019 instead and am completely satisfied with those two. Shades of butter, gold, apricot, tangerine, buff and parchment. What more could I ask for? Except health and fragrance? Check! Since we moved in, that bedroom has been the coolest room in the house, but we didn't because we like it cool to sleep. If the rest of the main level was set at 70, it typically stayed about 66 degrees. About two weeks ago, we noticed that the bedroom was suddenly much warmer than it had been. But when we left it open, the room still heated up. So last night I turned the heat down in the main section of the home and left the door open. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-11586870", "author_name": "John F", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-11586870", "date": "2022-03-29", "text": "EDIT: I am having issues uploading the picture here. So here is the imgur link: Click Here For Layout Hi, I want to add a bathroom to this space. I have a 6x6 space that can be made bigger (6x8.5) by using some space on top of stairs (the left side of the bathroom floor will be sloping from 0\" to 36\" or so). I thought I could use this by putting the vanity there, and accepting to have no under-counter storage. Here is my best attempt at maximizing the space. Would love to hear your thoughts as this could make it feel much roomier than a standard 6x6 bathroom. - No preference for bathroom door to be in common space or bedroom. This is a 1/1 unit, with only occasional guests. - Doors could be (maybe should?) be pocket doors. Preference on regular doors for sound transmission. - No bathtub needed. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "nancyinmich", "author_name": "Nancy in Mich", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nancyinmich", "date": "2022-03-30", "text": "Another option would be to have a pony wall over the last half of the shower, and put the sink there, next to the end of the shower.  You have 31\u201d for a vanity.  You can then use the box over the stairs as an extension counter for the person using the sink.  My concern with trying to put the sink over the stairs is would you have the room needed for the drain?  Also, where does your water plumbing go?  You need vertical room for those under a sink. I have a box like this in my kitchen.  Mine is low, somewhere around stool height, but above it and further into the wall, we put a book shelf for our cookbooks and we put a glass door over the bookshelf. So, if someone sat on the box, they would be leaning against a glass door.  Instead, we use it to hold the dog food bin and the knife block. If your box over the stairs ends up less than about 36\u201d high, you can put a floating shelf as the countertop and then have rolled-up towel storage under the counter. You could put some shelves there instead of a counter, or even some drawer storage.  But I think your vanity area will need some landing spots for toiletries while in use.  You can maybe put shelves on the left half of the stair box (with your back to the shower) and drawers on the right half. And I looked up the needed room for a toilet.  You need to have 15\u201d from a wall or any other bathroom fixture, measured from the centerline of the toilet.  That means you need at least 30\u201d width to have a toilet in the alcove by the door.  Some municipalities specify 18\u201d from the centerline in either direction.  Can you find the room?", "images": []}}

I grew up near the Ontario east of Los Angeles, so that is my first vision of a location when I see the word.  For your Canadian location you could either sod or seed this time of year.  For anyone south of you I would worry about crabgrass and the summer heat killing the new grass plants. As for your gate, I always use hardscape at a choke point like a gate or the landing at the bottom of steps.  Otherwise the grass will wear out and die. title: Food Floof! Making the cut! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "amylou321", "author_name": "amylou321", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/amylou321", "date": "2022-03-30", "text": "Sandwiches. Do you cut them? How and why? If it is a sandwich made on \"regular\" bread, that is from a sliced loaf, I tend to cut them straight across because I think that it the filling stays inside better that way, even though I prefer the the aesthetic   of them cut diagonally for no particular reason. If its something like a cheese steak on a hoagie roll or a sandwich on a baguette, or even a wrap, I cut it in half on a bias, because I feel fancier that way. If I make my own sandwich bread, its heart shaped and therefore cutting is forbidden. Same thing with homemade biscuits for a breakfast sandwich. Heart shaped and whole. What's the point otherwise? Sometimes, if its just for me, I just skip the cutting altogether. Some sandwiches, like a BLT or egg salad, just eat better whole. Things on buns like burgers or fried chicken sandwiches, I leave whole unless I am making it for SO to take with him somewhere and I cut it in half so It is easier to eat. Jedoch sind wir dann nicht mehr alleine auf dem Grundst\u00fcck. Es gibt hier und da Vorteile und hier und da Nachteile. Kann uns jemand beraten oder einen Architekten oder eine Baufirma empfehlen, die neutral einen beraten k\u00f6nnen/m\u00f6chten? Wir sitzen im Rhein-Main-Gebiet. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1293004073", "author_name": "habes-architektur", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1293004073", "date": "2022-03-30", "text": "Hallo Herr Vasiliu. Wenn Sie 90 m2 Wohnfl\u00e4che angeben, nehme ich an, dass Sie eigentlich Nettogrundfl\u00e4che meinten, also die Grundfl\u00e4che ohne die Konstruktionsfl\u00e4che.In der Wohnfl\u00e4che sind keine Treppen, und keine Technikr\u00e4ume enthalten. Eine kleine Rechnung: 90 m2 Nettogrundfl\u00e4che pro Geschoss bedeuten umgerechnet ca. 81 m2 Wohnfl\u00e4che und 112m2 Bruttogrundfl\u00e4che. Dies bedeutet grob ca. 337 m3 umbauten Raum bei 3m Geschossh\u00f6he. In der Geschossh\u00f6he sind die Decken und Dachkonstruktionen mit drin (Flachdach). Insgesamt w\u00e4ren das dann: 675 m3 Umbauter Raum (ganz grob) 225 m2 Bruttogrundfl\u00e4che 180 m2 Nettogrundfl\u00e4che 162 m2 Wohnfl\u00e4che Alles gesch\u00e4tzt. Jetzt die n\u00e4chste Annahme auf Grund von Preisen f\u00fcr die Kostengruppe 300 (Baukonstruktion) und 400 (technische Anlagen) aus dem Jahr 2021, f\u00fcr Einfamilienh\u00e4user, unterkellert, einfacher, mittlerer Standard: 400 \u20ac/m3 Umbauter Raum: 270.000 \u20ac 1.300 \u20ac/m2 Bruttogrundfl\u00e4che: 292.500 \u20ac 2.000 \u20ac/m2 Nettogrundfl\u00e4che: 360.000 \u20ac 2.100 \u20ac/m2 Wohnfl\u00e4che: 340.000 \u20ac Gemittelt ergibt das ca. 315.500 \u20ac f\u00fcr die KG 300 und 400. title: Using Groundcovers to Improve Soil Organic Content | Houzz Forum

Has anyone tried to grow a groundcover - such as a clover - around the roses to help condition the soil?  The taproots of some flowering groundcover plants should help to fix nitrogen deep in the soil and bring other micronutrients down into the soil.  When the plant dies, its taproots become a decaying organic matter for the soil.   It seems like there could be a good symbiosis here. I am using garden waste compost as a mulch, and that has helped greatly to slowly recover the plants.   The groundcover strategy would be in addition to the mulch and fertilizer.", "images": []}

LocationThe place where you put your aquaponic system is highly important for the way in which the plants and the fish will develop. In order to obtain great results you should make sure that the temperature from the room is not too high, nor too low, that there is enough light for the plants to prepare their food and that no wind or extreme weather conditions will reach them. Adding additivesThere are cases in which your fish may not provide all the nutrients needed for your plants. main_question: {"author_id": "brucesanders123", "author_name": "Bruce", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/brucesanders123", "date": "2022-03-31", "text": "We are building a pool with a spa that will be slightly under water like I have seen here on Houzz. My contractor mentioned that while they look great, you lose efficiency for obvious reasons. My question relates to the amount of efficiency loss  that others have experienced when going  in this direction? How much longer does the spa take to heat? Does the outflow of spa water in spa mode still keep a hot spa in winter for instance? Thanks in advance.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mystic-pools-llc-pfvwus-pf~881695109", "author_name": "Mystic Pools, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/swimming-pool-builders/mystic-pools-llc-pfvwus-pf~881695109", "date": "2022-04-01", "text": "If I understand the planned design, the spa is under water as part of the pool level? While it is a nice, sleek look, there is only one way to truly separate the spa from the pool when in the spa mode using this design. Builders have installed a collection tank that allows the water level to drop down below the rim of the spa, so it can run and heat independently when set is SPA. Otherwise, your just heating the water from the pool and the spa together, and it won't reach temperature. The collection tank must be sized accordingly to handle the volume of the water needed to drop down to the spa level. It's a tricky set up and a lot of calculations are required. There is additional plumbing and pumps to make this happen. Plus and additional structure of gunite must shot, or a fiberglass tank must be used. Consider a perimeter overflow spa that is set 2\"-3\" above the pool water. The top is constantly wet and provides a nice look.
